speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting the privileges of all hon. members. In Hansard for January 23 will be found an answer given by the Minister of Labour to a question I asked him-I am making this as brief as possible, sir-in which the minister states, as recorded on page 241, that the unemployment figure, the D.B.S. figure, for March, 1958, which he said was well known to me though in fact I do not carry all these figures in my head, was 509,000. He did not give more than the rough figure, and I do not criticize that. But, sir, on examining Labour Force, November, 1945, to July, 1958, reference paper No. 58, 1958 revision, published by the dominion bureau of statistics, the figure given for March 22, 1958 is 597,000. Therefore the minister was 90,000 out and in addition he was wrong in saying that this figure was lower than the figure in 1955.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: WINDSOR, ONT.-FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO BLIGHTED AREA CLEARANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that the federal government has approved a contribution to the city of Windsor under the National Housing Act to assist the municipality to acquire and clear a blighted area in the central portion of the city.
The proposals put forward by the city of Windsor envisage the clearance of an area of some 28 acres. Approximately one-half of this land, when cleared, will be sold by the city to the federal government and the province of Ontario for the construction of a low rental housing project consisting of some 280 units, the cost of which will be shared 75 per cent by the federal government and 25 per cent by the province in accordance with the provisions of section 36 of the National Housing Act. These units will provide accommodation for the families living in the area.
The remaining half of the land will be used for civic and institutional purposes as well as for private housing. The city has estimated that it will cost approximately $4,300,000 to acquire and clear this land. Under section 23 of the National Housing Act the federal government will contribute 50 per cent of the cost and will also share in any proceeds from the sale or lease of the land.
I am informed that the province of Ontario, in addition to its participation in the financing of the housing project, will also contribute financially to the cost of acquiring and clearing that portion of the area which will be used as the site for the housing project. The remainder of the acquisition and clearance cost will be borne by the city.
This project is bound to have an important impact on the structure of the central area of Windsor. It will provide additional employment opportunities as demolition progresses and a start is made on reconstruction but, above all, it will provide a new environment and new homes for approximately 1,000 persons. It is expected that the taking over of the land will commence almost immediately. This, of course, is in the hands of the city, and there will be expropriation and demolition. When the housing project itself 'is undertaken there will be a cost of probably $3 million. The project should be started during the summer.

subtopic: WINDSOR, ONT.-FEDERAL CONTRIBUTION TO BLIGHTED AREA CLEARANCE
speechtext: I thank the Minister of Public Works for making an announcement which, in principle, was made about five weeks ago by the mayor of Windsor. The regrettable feature of this of course, as the minister knows, is that the opportunity which this project provides for giving immediate work does not afford any relief in terms of the present unemployment. However, I should like to say to the minister that this project will be of great assistance to Windsor if not in the immediate future then in the longer term, and I thank the minister very much for his interest in making this project possible to a city which he recognizes as one of the outstanding cities in this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to add my congratulations to the many that have already been extended to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I should like to say to the hon. member for Provencher that I have been thoroughly indoctrinated in agricultural thinking, because I find I have little support in this particular section of the house. I also wish to extend congratulations to the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet who seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I want to thank him for the effort he made to bring about greater unity in Canada.
The speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was also particularly masterful 66968-9-241
in that his accusations against the government of fumbling and bumbling were a bold attempt to cover up what has plagued his party for a good many years. Some of his fellow members betrayed him rather badly in subsequent speeches. The Liberal party professes to be a free trade or low tariff and free enterprise party, but almost invariably its members cry in the house, if not directly then by inference, for tariff protection or federal financial assistance for industries in their own constituencies.
The Liberals got along fine as a government as long as Canadian industry had a sellers' market in a goods-hungry post-war world, as long as Canadian industry could keep pushing up the prices of its products to meet increasing costs created by spiralling inflation and taxation in the post-war years. But, Mr. Speaker, when we hit a buyers' market the Liberal balloon soon deflated, and it is going to take a lot of patching before they will ever get it into the air again. Speaking of fumbling and bumbling, they bumbled their way last night into supporting a socialist amendment in the house.
The leader of the C.C.F. group also did a good deal of fumbling in his half hour masterpiece. He talked about the plight of the poor farmers in Saskatchewan, that C.C.F.-governed province, and how inflation was squeezing the life out of them. Yet one of the leaders of his party, a former member of the house, advocates a policy for labour that must inevitably lead to increases in the cost of the goods and equipment that the farmers must buy.
I have every sympathy for the farmer. I was born on a farm, and as a boy I worked many a long day on the land. I worked on a Saskatchewan farm in the days of the harvest excursions, when men used to come from the far west and east to help in the harvesting of the crop. Those were the days of an earlier radical group known as the I.W.W. I refused to be prevailed upon by members of that group to throw a pitchfork into the separator, weary as I was sometimes and tempted to do so.
I have been in Saskatchewan several times in recent years, and I spent some time there last fall. I drove through most of the agricultural area of Saskatchewan, even getting up to their prosperous timber area. I am a fairly observant person, but I did not see any evidence of the dire poverty and distress that we hear so much about in the house from the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I hope, Mr. Speaker, that I can be broadminded enough not to condemn all the farmers of Saskatchewan if the proposed march to Ottawa takes place by some of them who have been whipped into mob

The Address-Mr. McQuillan hysteria by irresponsible people both in and out of Saskatchewan. I do not know where they think the money will come from to give them approximately $250 million in so-called deficiency payments which they are demanding. I do not think they really care. Perhaps they are naive enough to think it can come from increased taxation of other Canadian industries. They may even think that it can come from an industry with which I have been connected for a great part of my life. I refer to the forest industry.
I wish to speak about the forest industry for a few minutes. I think most hon. members are aware that the forest industry is by far the biggest employer of industrial labour in Canada. It provides a larger share of the payroll for Canada's industrial labour force than any other industry. It has the biggest capital investment in plant and equipment and is responsible by far for a greater part of Canada's export trade than any other segment of our economy. Its exports amount to approximately $1J billion annually, or 30 per cent of Canada's total exports.
The industry has weathered the recession fairly well, largely through its own initiative in selling to export markets, and this despite the fact that our lumber exporters, mostly centered in British Columbia, have had to face a 20 per cent drop in export market prices during the last two years in order to meet world competition. The industry has been primarily responsible for the fact that unemployment in British Columbia, according to the latest figures, has not worsened over what it was at this time last year. In fact on my last check I found that there was considerable improvement in my own constituency. If mother nature does not throw too much snow, such as we are getting in Ottawa, on British Columbia's coast, I believe we can look for considerable improvement in the province's employment picture.
The forest industry is the highest taxed in the nation in two of Canada's major producing provinces, Ontario and British Columbia. This is because of discriminatory provincial income taxes that are a legacy of provincial tax-sharing agreements made by the former federal government, which left the way open for money-hungry provincial premiers to impose income taxes over and above those levied against any other industry. The royal commission on Canada's economic prospects stated in its report:
-Canadians must guard against overrating the strength of their position in forest and mineral products: for most of such commodities, there are many closely competitive sources in other parts of the world.
[Mr. McQuillan.1
I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance that the first step in implementing this recommendation of the Gordon commission would be for him to help these industries to rid themselves of the iniquitous, discriminatory taxes from which they suffer in the two provinces I have mentioned. I know that in British Columbia these taxes are discouraging much potential new capital investment which would go a long way toward beating the unemployment problem there. In my opinion that is the right way to defeat the unemployment problem.
I also suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that his department should spare no effort and, indeed, that they should extend themselves in helping the forest industry to maintain and expand its markets. Sometimes I get the impression from statements made in the house that the only export commodity Canada has is grain. I should like to remind the house and particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there are many other commodities with respect to which the officials of his department could extend themselves. These forest markets are British Columbia's living.
In view of the tremendous part that the forest industry plays in Canada's economy I should like to make a suggestion to the Prime Minister, and I hope he will not treat it lightly. I think the time is long overdue for a government department which is primarily concerned with Canada's forests and forest industries. Some of you might think I am looking for a job, but that is far from my mind. The need for this department is obvious if one just reads the trade statistics.
Another problem which faces our forest industries in British Columbia, and a very pressing one, is that of freight rates. If I might misquote a song from the musical play "Oklahoma", that last one was about as far as we can go, in fact it was a little bit farther than we can afford to go. If there were another such increase we would be faced with the loss of most of our rail markets. I do think it is high time we faced our railway problems realistically. It may be that we will have to sacrifice some of our unnecessary and costly passenger or freight services throughout the country. We must hold the line on freight rates or our export industries will soon find themselves priced out of their markets. If the prairie grain producers need, and I do not dispute that they need, special consideration in the form of the Crowsnest pass freight rates, then I do not believe it is fair that other exporters should have to pay for this special treatment.
While on the subject of freight rates, I may say that on the Pacific coast we have a coastal

freight rate problem which I am afraid is worsening very quickly. Up to last spring we had three major steamship companies serving the British Columbia coast-the Canadian Pacific, the Union Steamship Company, which served the coast for over 50 years, and the Northland company. I do not count the Canadian National. They have one luxury cruise ship which makes a few trips during the summer, but its sole contribution during the winter months for the last few years has been to provide accommodation for visiting Grey cup fans. For many years the Canadian Pacific and the Union Steamship Company received varying subsidies and did provide an excellent coastal service.
Shortly after the war the Northland Steamship Company entered the coastal service and last summer acquired two vessels from the Canadian Pacific, and the Canadian Pacific retired from the upper coastal area and the west coast of Vancouver island. It is my understanding that they agreed to stay out of these areas as long as the Northland company provides service. The management of the Northland company succeeded in arranging for quite a substantial subsidy from this government. The Union company, which had been operating without a subsidy since January 1958, continued operating but were unable to successfully negotiate a subsidy. Their financial position steadily worsened, to such an extent that a few days ago they found it necessary to sell their fleet to the Northland company. Now, instead of two or three junk fleets, we have one great big one. The Northland company now has a virtual monopoly of the British Columbia coastal steamship service, except from Nanaimo south along Vancouver island.
Recently I have received a number of communications on this subject, and I should like to read one or two excerpts from them. These are the first communications I have received, but I know there are many more to come. I have a telegram here from the village of Sointula on Malcolm island. It reads in part:
With the cessation of Union Steamship services last week we find that Sointula is deprived of southbound passenger service entirely. Northbound being restricted to eight passengers on a tramp freighter which accommodation is intended to take care of other ports besides. This situation is ridiculous and we trust that you will take it up with the Minister of Transport for early correction.
I have another letter here from a man who has spent his life in the upper coastal area where he and his son operate a small sawmill. He says:
Again we are being thrown to the wolves. Yesterday we were informed by the Union Steamship Company that they were being taken over by the Northland company and that the Catala was off
The Address-Mr. McQuillan
the run. We were also notified that our mail and perishable freight would be delivered either at Alert Bay or Beaver Cove as we wished, but no days yet announced.
It goes on to say many more things, and he informs me that if I do not do something about this I will not be down here after the next election. He is quite justified in telling me that.
There will be disruptions and cancellation of service, as well as rapidly increasing freight rates. They have a little gimmick in coastal freight rates in that they have cubic and per ton rates. I do not know just who decides whether an article is to take the cubic or per ton rate, but 40 cubic feet are supposed to represent a ton. Wherever there is no competition the steamship company uses the cubic rate. As a result it simply means that to send 100 loaves of bread a couple of hundred miles up the coast it will cost somewhere between 6 cents and 10 cents a loaf. I have another letter here from a man who lives 100 miles north of Vancouver, in which he points out that it costs him $24.70 to get 1,000 feet of lumber from Vancouver.
As I said before, there will be disruptions and cancellation of service, as well as rapidly increasing freight rates, unless the government provides subsidies in order to maintain the rates at their present level. These subsidies are going to be on the Northland company's terms, or there will be no service or freight rates will be so exorbitant they will seriously jeopardize the economy of many communities and undoubtedly drive many businesses and residents out of the area. This is an area, Mr. Speaker, which is one of the first to have a short labour supply whenever there is anything resembling prosperous conditions in the country, because of the isolation and the fact that people with families do not want to live there. This area produces much of the raw material for the plywood plants and other industries on Vancouver island and the lower mainland.
I have been concerned for the past year about the possibility of such a situation as has arisen, and have repeatedly brought the matter to the attention of the minister concerned and some of his officials. However, the concern seemed to be all mine, and here we are with the worst coastal transportation problem in British Columbia's history staring us right in the face. I should like to tell Vancouver members to take an interest in this matter, because if those mills in their constituencies run out of logs because no one will live up the coast to produce them, they are going to have an unemployment problem that will make their present one look like prosperity.

The Address-Mr. Bourget
Even without any deterioration of the coastal service as it has existed for the past few months there is the matter of the mail service to many of the small coastal communities, which is a source of annoyance and inconvenience. Some of the communities are fortunate enough to have first class air mail service, while others receive their mail by infrequent boat service. This situation exists despite the fact that small float planes shuttling passengers to and from Port Hardy airport frequently pass by all these communities. I have taken this matter up with the Postmaster General, and he has undertaken to investigate it and have a report made.
The second class mail constitutes a real problem. Very few people in that area subscribe to newspapers any longer, because by the time they get them they are perhaps 10 days or two weeks old. One woman told me that second class mail service is so poor that when she ordered a pair of shoes for one of her children, by the time she received the shoes the child had outgrown them.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to compliment this government, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, and in particular the Minister of Trade and Commerce, for the lead they took in arranging for the commonwealth trade conference held in Montreal last fall. There is no question but that this was a worth-while conference. Much was accomplished and I think much more can be accomplished by another one in the near future. I would suggest that the motto be to have a commonwealth trade conference again in 1959.

Mr. Speaker, before saying what I have to say about the address in reply, may I tell you how happy

I am that you are again presiding over the proceedings of this house. I am confident that, as in the past, you will be doing so with tact, judgment, impartiality and at the same time with some leniency.
I should also like to mention, Mr. Speaker, that one of our colleagues who took sick some ten days ago is with us today, and back in good health. I refer to the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter).
I too would like to join the previous speakers in extending congratulations to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) of the address in reply who spoke knowingly of the problems of his electors, who are farmers. I think he performed his task in responsible and eloquent fashion.
As to the seconder of the address, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) a distinguished son of the constituency of Levis which I have the honour to represent here, I want to say that his was an excellent speech. I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that he will follow in the footsteps of his father and grandfather, and will worthily represent the constituency of Mont-magny-L'Islet.
I was particularly happy to hear it stated by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet that he considers the province of Quebec to be like any other province. It was something new, Mr. Speaker, because ever since we have had the Union Nationale in the province of Quebec, I do not recall having heard a French-Canadian Conservative member of the province make such a statement. I congratulate him, because he thereby recognized that we Liberals, in the past, were right to say that the province of Quebec is a province like all other provinces. I hope, for the good of our fellow citizens, that these words will not only be repeated but acted upon.
May I be allowed also, Mr. Speaker, to refer to the presence this morning in the gallery of our good friends from Montreal, the radio and T.V. employees, who, despite their long drive of 120 miles, despite the hardships they have put up with these last four weeks, seem to me, although I can only see them some distance away, to still display that smile that we are so happy to see on our T.V. screens in the province of Quebec. Well, may I give them a word of encouragement. I believe there is a glimmer of hope for them, because yesterday, following the questions

asked by the member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) who, since the beginning of the session, together with his colleagues from Montreal in particular, has shown interest in their problem, a minister has said here yesterday, and even has repeated today that their strike is not illegal.
My colleague from Gloucester, N.B. (Mr. Robichaud), has just been telling me that His Eminence Cardinal Paul-Emile Leger, Archbishop of Montreal, referred to the C.B.C. producers' strike in an address given yesterday evening before the alumni of College Ste. Marie. His Eminence stated, and I quote:
Like the Ste. Marie alumni, everyone has the right of association. The C.B.C. strike is nothing else than that. That right, and we have examples of this every day, must be asserted.
Since we were told yesterday and again to-day by a minister of the crown that this strike is not illegal, there is every reason to hope that, in due course, the government will do something or, at least, will agree to the hon. member for Laurier's request that the negotiating committee on radio be convened at once to hear this case and the government's case at the same time.
At any rate, on behalf of my colleagues, I welcome these visitors and hope that their stay among us will be as fruitful for them, their families as for all those who, in Frenchspeaking communities in Canada, and particularly in the province of Quebec, are anxious to see these smiling faces again on television.

When the hon. member for Roberval wishes to have the floor, he can have it. I must tell him that I am not in the habit of interrupting other members. I have been sitting in this house for 19 years, and I do not think I have a reputation for butting in. When I put a question to the person who has the floor, I at least have the courtesy to ask his permission.
Mr. Chairman, I shall go on with my remarks.
I was saying that I wanted to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply, and also Mr. Speaker. However, I am sorry I cannot so heartily congratulate the government which has been managing the affairs of Canada since June 1957.
Since the opening of this debate, our leader and other Liberal members have shown up with undeniable evidence the weaknesses of the present administration.
In the few minutes I have at my disposal, I should like to deal chiefly with one of the most significant problems of the day, unemployment, and particularly to analyse, in the restricted field of unemployment, the effectiveness of the winter works program put forth by the federal government.
The letter that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) sent to members of parliament last November 20-informing them of the government's proposals to the provinces in connection with the campaign for the promotion of winter employment in the municipalities, was accompanied by a copy of the letters he had sent to the various provincial premiers, outlining the same program. In these letters to the premiers, the Minister of Labour stated in detail the conditions governing the federal government's offer. There were fifteen conditions, and the third listed the types of allowable projects, subject to acceptance of each winter works project. Among the projects that could be undertaken by municipalities and in which the government agreed to share the costs, were the following:
(a)	Construction and major reconstruction of streets, sidewalks and roads, except main highways.
(b)	Construction and major reconstruction of waterworks, sewers and storm sewers, not including buildings.
(c)	Construction and development of municipal parks.
Later on, the following were added:
Municipal playgrounds, whether located inside or outside a municipal park, excluding school playgrounds.

For these classes of acceptable projects, the government of Canada, subject to approval of each project by the provincial government, will refund to each municipality one-half the direct cost to the municipality (or to its contractors or subcontractors) of salaries paid during the period from December 1, 1958 to April 30, 1959 for the carrying out of accepted winter works covered by this proposal.
Such was the outline of the offer made by the federal government to the provinces for its winter works program. The program was widely publicized, the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) even gave a talk about it on television on December 22 last-the producers were not on strike at the time. In the course of his remarks he said among other things:
However, the Diefenbaker government has taken every possible step for relieving unemployment on a large scale. This comes as a surprise to many Canadians. The Liberals had accustomed them to another, somewhat ostrich-like, policy. The ministers were content to deny that there was any unemployment, leaving provincial governments, municipalities and individuals to face the problem.
No matter how much we protested, or pointed out all kinds of dangers and threats that could easily have been met or averted, the previous administration always disclaimed responsibility. For them it was enough to say for instance: "We must not allow ourselves to be intimidated by the fear of unemployment, leaving provincial governments, unemployed, provincial governments and municipalities.
The response of the Diefenbaker government has been different. It has not eluded the problem. It has accepted it and is doing its level best to find an adequate solution.
Mr. Speaker, I point out that the Secretary of State claimed that the government had not eluded the problem, but then I say to the Secretary of State that the government did not solve the problem either.
Before going any further, I want to tell the hon. Secretary of State that if we Liberals had accustomed the people of Canada to an ostrich-like policy, we certainly did not keep our heads buried in the sand as long as did the Conservatives, because workers never had to put up with as much unemployment as there has been since the Conservatives took power.
I wonder also if before delivering his address, the hon. Secretary of State carefully considered the practical impact of this winter employment program on the unemployed and the municipalities of this country.
Before telling him exactly what this means, I would like, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words on the background of the unemployment question. We recall, no doubt, that during the fall of 1957, when employment was growing alarmingly, Liberal members, one after the other were trying to induce the government

to take the necessary steps to alleviate the situation. Contrary to what the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) said in his talk it was not the Liberals who were in power then but the Conservatives, and the Conservatives were the ones who refuse to admit that there was unemployment then. And, it is only by the end of January, on the eve of the general election, that the Conservative government recognized that the country had unemployment and that the situation was becoming alarming. It is then that it admitted the existence of unemployment and claimed that if there was, it was the fault of the former administration. On March 31, during the election, the hon. Secretary of State as well as the other ministers and the Conservative members from the province of Quebec and the rest of the country emphasized the famous special public works program which was to cost $1,185 millions. Well, Mr. Speaker, we realized soon afterwards that the famous special undertaking of public works costing $1,185 million, publicized over television and radio, existed only in the minds of our opponents, because in the final analysis the amount of $1,185 million which was mentioned represented only the sum total of the amounts spent each year by every department which performs construction work. And, furthermore, the bulk of the projects included in that program of $1,185 million had been conceived and developed by the former Liberal administration.
Subsequently, during the session which opened in May of last year the Liberal opposition asked the government on different occasions to take the necessary steps to spare thousands of Canadian workers the distress they had to suffer during the winter months of 1957-58. It was only in July, on the 14th and 15th of July, to be exact Mr. Speaker, that a national conference on winter employment was called last year in Ottawa. Representatives of all provinces, and representatives of many Canadian associations, workers' unions, industries along with prominent economists took part in this conference. It seems to me that, after that conference, when the government could have taken advantage of the suggestions offered by that group of persons, the people of Canada were entitled to expect the government to come up with a faster and more generous solution than the one I mentioned in my earlier remarks. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the offer came too late because, according
The Address-Mr. Bourget to the letter of the Minister of Labour to the provincial premiers, it was only in October, three months after the conference took place in Ottawa, that the provincial premiers were informed by telegram of the offer the federal government wished to make.
Anyone who has some knowledge of municipal affairs knows in the first place, that it takes several weeks to survey the sites, to draw up plans and specifications, to have them approved by council, to call for tenders and to go ahead with the work. Moreover, and I am referring to my province in particular, I must say that it was only on December 11 or 12, three weeks after the provincial session opened in Quebec, that the Union Nationale government enacted legislation authorizing municipalities to take part in this project and giving them the right to borrow the necessary funds to carry out those works without referendum. This, Mr. Speaker, was a further three week delay after the already belated offer of federal authorities in regard to those works. But what is even worse, in my opinion, than the delay in announcing this program, is the futility of the reimbursement offer made by the federal government to the municipalities. As a matter of fact, and still according to information provided by the hon. minister, the federal government agrees to repay to each municipality half of total salaries paid between December 1, 1958 and April 30, 1959. Now, Mr. Speaker, as an engineer with some experience in the type of works referred to in this offer, I can state positively with many others that labour costs in those various projects represent at most 20 per cent of the total costs of works when performed in the summer. I would not like to venture an opinion on the higher cost of winter works in the other provinces since I did not practise my profession in those provinces. However, I do know from experience that, in the province of Quebec, and particularly in our area, winter works cost from 15% to 20% more. This increase, Mr. Speaker is made up of higher labour costs amounting roughly to 80 per cent; and 4 per cent higher cost of materials, machinery, "borrowed material" and other things to which the government offer does not apply because the government is not paying anything as regards materials or machinery.
Let me give you as an example a waterworks project. I use that example because I think that, in Quebec or other parts of

The Address-Mr. Bourget Canada where almost the same climate conditions prevail, it would be quite difficult, to undertake anything but waterworks and sewer projects. Let us say, for example, that a municipal corporation has in mind some waterworks project which would ordinarily cost $100,000, i.e. $20,000 for labour and $80,000 for equipment and material. The same work done in the wintertime will cost $119,200, i.e. $36,000 for labour and $83,200 for equipment, materials, etc. Then, in the present case, under the federal offer, the municipal corporation would get 50 per cent for labour, 50 per cent on $36,000, or $18,000. The municipality will therefore have to pay an extra $1,200, i.e. the difference between $19,200 and the $18,000 it will get from the federal government.
I don't believe it can be said that the government has been over-generous and that our municipalities should be enthusiastic over that highly publicized offer. The example I just gave is based first on my own experience of municipal works and my opinion is corroborated by studies made by the city of Quebec technical services on some projects which they propose to submit to the federal government.
In the paper Le Soleil of December 17, 1958, there is an article which reads as follows:
Quebec will launch a $500,000 works program to cut down unemployment.
Two days later, on December 19, the same paper published an editorial entitled:
The city-

And here is a part of the article that will be of great interest to hon. members. I quote:
Municipal authorities have decided to take advantage of the federal law which provides financial assistance to municipalities for winter works projects to reduce unemployment throughout the country. The council's decision was not taken in a surge of enthusiasm. Council members resigned themselves to the idea with the conviction that it was only a lesser evil. Explanations which were given at the last council meeting when a list was drawn up of works to be undertaken in mid-January,-
And, according to the latest information, these works will be undertaken only by mid-February. Then-
-showed that municipal authorities are convinced that they are making a bad deal. The works amounting roughly to $500,000 will yield $186,000 in salaries. From 100 to 200 persons will be employed for about three and a half months.


I repeat, 100 or 200 persons, when there must be at least 15,000 unemployed in the city of Quebec. They will employ from 100 to 200 persons during two or three and a half months.
Even if the federal government is to pay half of the labour cost, the city would spend $5,000 more on that works program than if the work had been done during the summer, at the city's own expense. It is obvious that this initiative on the part of the city which it could hardly avoid taking, will be of little help in relieving unemployment within the city. A small fraction only of our unemployed will benefit from it, and on the whole it will be a very slight impetus to the Quebec economy in general.
That is why council members said that the federal legislation is inadequate.
Furthermore, the mayor of Quebec stated the following, as recorded in Le Soleil of December 1958. I quote:
The city is undertaking those projects solely to help the unemployed; in fact, from the administrative point of view, the city is not making a good deal.
This seems to me a good example to bring forward at this time. Besides, other municipalities are reacting in the same way. After all they fully realize that they will be called upon to pay 100 per cent or even more of the costs of the works which they would decide to undertake in the course of that period.
I should like to add that in the province of Quebec municipalities are worse off than elsewhere; indeed in certain provinces, like Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, it was deemed proper, no doubt after considering the program and what I would call the federal government's measly offer to municipalities, to contribute additional amounts varying between 25 to 30 per cent of the cost of salaries.
In the province of Quebec, the Union Na-tionale government usually proves itself quite large-handed when awarding contracts, yet it did not see fit to vote a penny to assist the 175,000 or 200,000 unemployed we now have in the province. However, the provincial government keeps repeating, especially in election time, that the financial situation of the province is just fine, that it is the best of all provinces in the confederation. Well then, why not help out the municipalities under the circumstances?
In the past our opponents consistently claimed that the responsibility for a solution to the unemployment problem lay mainly at the door of the federal government. Well,

it is a sad thing to see this fast reversal of policy, since after all, as I said, the share paid by the federal government in those projects is nominal and, in the province of Quebec, the financial assistance given by the Union Nationale government is nil. As was so pointedly stated last Wednesday by the hon. member for Laurier, it is certainly not with four, six or eight million dollars that we can hope to improve the situation of the 600,000 unemployed in Canada.
I was therefore correct in saying that this federal government project, like last year's famed public works program, is nothing but eyewash.
I shall be urged to be objective, to state what solution the Liberal party would have offered under the circumstances. I see that my speaking time is running short, but I would suggest that my hon. friends look up the program that the Liberal party offered to the Canadian people in the last election. They will see, in the section dealing with aid to the municipalities, what we would have done, they will find that we would have paid a greater part of the total cost of the works, so as not to let the full burden rest, once again, on the municipalities, which, Mr. Speaker, now have to pay at least six, and in certain cases up to seven per cent interest on loans.
In my constituency, no municipality is sharing in this program, because they cannot afford it. I know that my hon. friends opposite share my view in this regard and realize that our municipalities, particularly in the province of Quebec, cannot afford to share in this program. The reason is not, Mr. Speaker, that we have no unemployment, no cases of hardship. Actually, in mid-December 1958, there were 4,447 applicants registered at the Levis office, and the figure must now have reached close to 6,000, not including those who have not registered.
I said a moment ago that we would have contributed a larger share of the total cost of the works. In fact this government could have done as much if it had known how to manage those expenditures wisely, without any extra cost to the Canadian taxpayer. It only had to grant j of 1 per cent less interest on the bonds of the last conversion loan. This would have meant a saving of at least 15 to 20 million dollars which could have been applied to this winter work program. But this was not done, Mr. Speaker, because it is quite apparent that, since they took office, our friends opposite have no time to think; they are satisfied with proceeding on a piecemeal basis.
The Address-Mr. Tremblay
As I said, this government must take the blame for its lack of action and for having no definite projects in mind to alleviate the problems which we must meet, and also for failing to take steps which were imperative.
Mr. Speaker, I hope I shall not be told that my approach has been merely negative. On the contrary I have tried, during those few minutes at my disposal, to be as unbiased as possible in showing the weaknesses of that program while suggesting one way to solve the problem or at least to improve in a substantial way the winter works program now submitted to the population by the Conservative government.

commercial activity would slow down to a level of stability. This quest for stability was necessarily accompanied by some groping and uneasiness characterized by a more or less severe recession. Mr. Speaker, before recess, I was saying that the Liberals had deluded the Canadian people by saying: "We will put an end to the recession and to unemployment." I added that it was a well-known fact that when the international situation had slowly recovered due to war preparations, the Liberals had still done nothing to assist the population so that the new Quebec government, from 1936 on, had to give direct assistance to the people of our province through public works and social security measures.
The war in 1939 saved the Liberals who were haunted by the depression and unemployment. The people credited them with Canadian prosperity until, around 1955 and 1956, they saw our economy floundering. They worried to the point of asking the Conservative party to take over in June 1957.
This time the Liberal party will not be able by means of a smear campaign to grasp control over the nation's affairs. People are watching, day by day, the work of the government they elected. They realize that this government is going out of its way to find efficient remedies to the evils which beset us. Above all, they accept the sacrifices made necessary by the nation's economic recovery. They do this to follow the example set by other countries which must also, in order to face their difficulties, impose on their taxpayers a regime of austerity; such is the case in Argentina and in France.
Another thing that people see is the unhealthy use being made by the opposition of the difficulties facing the government and the citizens. Political capital is being made of unrest, unemployment, and the suffering of citizens. Politics are being played with matters which, on the contrary, should call for reflection, sympathy and positive action. What have we been hearing here since the debates have been resumed? Cries of alarm, affected indignation, hypocritical profession of faith in principles of humanity and social benevolence so often betrayed and despised. Who spoke about unemployment in a way to unduly frighten the Canadian people? Who moaned, cried, vociferated about imminent catastrophes and irreparable disasters?
This show of assumed compassion has been given us by seasoned actors, by men who know every trick of expediency and artifice.


Mr. Speaker, one of the beneficial effects of this sadistic propaganda was to disgust an hon. member of the opposition who seems to be a member of that party without being one of its supporters. I quote him from Hansard of January 22, 1959, page 19 of the English appendix:
I do not wish to play politics with unemployment. Too many members in this house use this calamity to play politics.
And later, he added:
X believe that we should consider the question of unemployment from a human point of view and try to find a solution.
This was, Mr. Speaker, the voice of reason, of common sense, and in a word, of decency.
This call to order was bound to ring out amidst the shrieks of political passion. And it is interesting to note that that intervention came from the most fanatical of the opposition groups. Within the Liberal camp, such a note must really be too jarring, but in any event, it reveals that after two sessions, several Liberals have reached the point of saturation. There is certainly a new trend in the making, a trend which we feel sure will be in the direction of honesty and fair play.
We hope, for our part, that this change of heart on the opposition side will result in positive suggestions being made, instead of the bitter and negative criticisms we have been hearing so far. Indeed, it must be recognized that if, in fact, the situation of this country is as tragic as it is being represented to the people, it must also be admitted, Mr. Speaker, that we have been left alone to improve it. Who, in the opposition, has come forward with practical suggestions? Oh, of course, Mr. Speaker, there have been suggestions! The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) stated, for instance, to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr): "It is your business". And the improbable member for Hull (Mr. Caron) who, as the man in the fable, would have pumpkins grow on oak trees, advanced the suggestion that to end unemployment Her Majesty the Queen, when she visits Canada, should pat Canadian babies on the cheek. On that occasion, he wrote this statement, which is well worthy of the dadaist school, and I quote from page 197 of Hansard:
And when the Queen Mother went by, so close to the people, a woman held up her baby and the Queen Mother went up to the child and patted it.
Imagine the feelings of this mother seeing the Sovereign of Canada go up to her baby.

Mr. Speaker, with all due deference to Her Majesty, I do not believe that the proposal of the hon. member for Hull could in any way relieve the present unemployment situation.
Who did provide us with suggestions for restoring the Canadian economy? The Liberals claim that they have always been wise and careful administrators. Have they? If this is so, why don't they put their wisdom and their experience at the service of the citizens and of the government? Do we have to corner them into doing it? Where are the improvident administrators that the people have condemned twice, in 1957 and 1958, and, in this case, why do they criticize and why do they spread confusion in the minds of citizens? If they are experts in the field of administration, they have no right to deprive the government of their valuable advice.
It must be admitted that the Liberals' contribution to the people of Canada has been rather poor these last few months. This contribution has amounted to no more than the selfsame grievances, voiced by the Liberal chieftains, parroted by the party's rank and file, and heeded only by professional agitators, whose function is to spread trouble and strife.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I am amazed at the similarity of the methods of those who, in Canada, incite aggressive claims, manage to insinuate themselves into our labour organizations, capitalize on the difficulties and disputes that happen between employers and employees, and the methods used by marxist propagandists.
This similarity is evident in their common desire to create disturbance in the minds and conscience of people, to alarm citizens by setting up the cry of real or fancied injustice. This first step is soon followed by the running down of authorities at all levels. They work on the principle that authorities always favour the strong, that the weak are necessarily always right, and that whatever governments might do, they will never be able to restore equity. This is the normal process of an impulse which, bred in the discontent which it has managed to create, leads to aggressive claims through direct attacks on authority and an assault against law and order.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I know what weakness and cowardice can often hide behind those words:	order and authority. But
beyond the people and individuals who, at a given time, hold the power, there is a principle which must be preserved, that of authority without which all is disorder and
The Address-Mr. Tremblay anarchy. I believe the time has come in this country to think about safeguarding this most important asset of society. Let anyone induce people to lose confidence in the institutions which govern them, and the decisive step has been taken towards irreparable social catastrophes. And here I am reminded of the warning given by Cardinal Leger in his recent pastoral letter on unemployment, and I quote:
Labour unions may try through collective action to interest public opinion in their legitimate claims provided however that truth, justice and charity are always respected. Organizations must keep away from demagogy which is always an obstacle to genuine solutions, generates an unhealthy climate of class struggle and uselessly and dangerously increases bitterness and resentment. The activity of the organizations must tend to enlighten the minds and stimulate the wills towards practical achievements. This is the climate that will generate an authentic spirit of co-operation without which there can be no real solution.
This appeal in favour of honesty, truth and charity is not directed solely to labour organizations but to all those who, in some degree, are responsible for government and public opinion.
It seems to me that the press, particularly a certain leftist press that will not let up until it has undermined order in Canada, should take this appeal to heart. Opposition members, in particular, should ponder those words, because they suggest a straightforward policy which does not exclude sound and constructive criticism, differences of opinions, re-examination of some problems and the criticism of institutions and of the men who operate them.
Those words of Cardinal Leger put us again in the face of our duties, the least of which does consist in trying to spare our country the political and social mistakes which paved the way to marxism in many countries. In that connection, Mr. Speaker, I should like to impart to you certain thoughts that occurred to me following my stay in New York as Canadian delegate to the General Assembly of the United Nations. And I take this opportunity to thank the Prime Minister, in my own name and on behalf of my constituents, for thus honouring the constituency of Roberval.
The time I spent there enabled me to realize more fully the threat of communism to world peace. I realized that the efforts of official diplomacy cannot alone defeat communist ideology. We must, by our example and by positive action, show to the world a

I therefore called upon my constituents to lend their support to our government's participation in the plan to give technical assistance and aid to underdeveloped countries. This is what I said on that occasion:
The communist regime is largely the product of social injustice. It is the responsibility of the countries that still understand the value of spiritual ideas to remove, in so far as possible, the causes of hardship and injustice. That is the only way in which we can defeat an atheistic and materialistic ideology that promises people their freedom and lures the meek by the false promise of illusory happiness born of equality among all classes of society. This task prompts us to share fully in the assistance and international mutual aid program. We can no longer afford to lag behind. It behooves us to provide our financial share and it is in this fashion that we shall contribute to the achievement of world peace.
If my colleague of the constituency of Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) had heard me that evening, he would not have stated so firmly the other night that no Conservative members from Quebec had yet pronounced itself on that question of assistance to under-developed countries.
I can only explain his attitude by his unawareness of that fact, because I know he is honest enough not to wilfully hide the truth. Besides, he belongs to a different school and is of different background from those of several colleagues of his party, those young and even not so young demagogues who will never learn, during the debates, to remain at the level of the principles of politics, history, political economy, legal economy and social


philosophy. And may I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I am ashamed to hear fellow-citizens of my province expressing themselves like anarchists when it comes to anything concerning Quebec, its prerogatives, its traditions and its institutions. I do not believe they rise in anybody's esteem by smearing those who control our affairs in Quebec. That they do not share the political beliefs of their opponents, that is their privilege, as men and citizens, but this does not give them the right to smear and insult the people of Canada who, by democratic means, have chosen their government.
Mr. Speaker, the exercise of democracy as we know it entails one handicap: that of electing to power, among fair-minded men, among men imbued with sound ideas and principles, dubious individuals and political adventurers. Fortunately, in this field also, immanent justice eventually prevails and only in rare cases do vituperators like those we have heard in recent days, last very long. They are soon swept out by the same wave which had momentarily held them afloat.
Last year, during the budget debate, I said that we, Conservatives from Quebec, have no lessons to learn from the Liberals. I was emphasizing in particular constitutional facts and problems. I was stating especially that the difficulties we are now encountering in this field are due to the fact that the Liberal party has forced the constitutional development of our country. This phenomenon has taken concrete form in the constitutional solutions of the Liberal party, and the least that can be said about them is that they are not always wholly in keeping with the nature and spirit of the British North America Act.
Thus it is, for instance, that adepts of Canadian neo-federalism are slyly attempting to shift the objectives of constitutional struggles. They would substitute an economic system contingent in itself, and subject to the changing conditions of our national economy, to a constitutional formula which in itself has a much more permanent value, for it is founded upon the lines of force of our history and the essential factors of the psychology of our ethnical groups. The undertaking is significant, but how perilous.
I submit that the Liberals are ill-advised in plying us with questions on constitutional problems and especially on fiscal problems. They need not fear. We shall, in due course stand by our convictions. Their experience will probably help us to avoid serious mistakes. In particular have we nothing to learn from Liberal members from Quebec?

Too long have they been tongue-tied on this subject, for us to be so naive as to believe the moon is made of green cheese. They are now like the monkey operating the magic lantern, save that they too have forgotten to light the lamp. The pronouncements made by the right hon. Prime Minister on education should sufficiently indicate to them that the Conservative party is intent on abiding by the constitution of this country. The representations made by the Liberal opposition will leave us unimpressed. It takes time to iron out certain delicate issues: it takes time and thought because a problem of such moment does not admit of a rash solution.
Last year, the most obscure and the most mixed up member of the Liberal party tried to take the Conservative members from the province of Quebec by surprise by asking for a vote after an inane speech that will remain as a model of what can come out of sheerest ignorance. After saying that the French element had died in 1760, after picking all concepts to pieces-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not apologize for rising to take part in this debate for a second time. I wish this afternoon to discuss two questions which affect in a special manner the citizens of the province of Quebec, but before I do so I hope the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat and who has complained so bitterly about the language used by hon. members on this side of the house, and especially about the language used by the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget), will not complain when I say to him that the language he has used has gone far beyond reason and that suggested by the hon. member who spoke this morning.
So far as his remarks with regard to myself are concerned, I pay not the slightest attention to them. The reason is that I hold my seat in this house as a member from the

The Address-Mr. Chevrier province of Quebec and as the member for the constituency of Laurier, and I have no lesson to learn from the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat. Furthermore, if the hon. member thinks he is going to teach anyone in this house a lesson by the kind of language he has used this afternoon he is entirely mistaken, because all he has done is go to the other extreme; and I say to him this: there are none so blind as those who will not see.
The first matter to which I should like to call the attention of the house is one which is to my mind of considerable importance not only to the people of Canada as a whole but in a particular degree to the people of the province of Quebec. I refer to the Chicago water diversion scheme. There has been some discussion of this in the house, and perhaps I can go over the matter again very briefly. By virtue of a decree issued in the United States supreme court it was provided that on and after December 31, 1938, the diversion of water from lake Michigan through the Chicago canal should be limited to 1,500 c.f.s. in addition to domestic pumping for the city of Chicago. Ever since that decree was made by the supreme court, Chicago and the metropolitan sanitary district of that community have sought to increase the diversion permitted; and while it was increased very slightly in 1940, in 1942 and again in 1944, the additional amount, I am told by the authorities, was not serious.
Since then, however, there have been three bills introduced into congress seeking to authorize an additional diversion of 1,000 c.f.s. Two of those bills have been vetoed by the President. In 1954 one bill was vetoed by the president. In 1955 another similar bill died. In 1956 the President vetoed a further bill and finally, in 1958, a bill failed to pass the Senate.
There is now before congress, as this house knows, another bill known as H.R. No. 1, the purpose of which is to divert an additional amount of water from lake Michigan into the Chicago drainage canal, which would have a serious and detrimental impact on downriver rights. Here I should like to refer to a question I asked of the Secretary of State for External Affairs on January 21, which will be found on page 148 of Hansard:

Is it not a fact that according to a study made by a subcommittee of the international joint commission power development in the international section will be materially affected by this diversion, and that the water level in Montreal will be reduced by three-quarters of an inch?

I must emphasize in reply that the Canadian government did make lengthy representations in writing which are contained in an aide memoire to the United States Department of State of January 6, 1958 and which, as I said on Wednesday, was tabled in this house on August 2, 1958.
The aide memoire registered the serious and deep concern of the government with respect to the injurious consequences which would result from any considerable diversion of water from the great lakes system.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext:
It did, sir; in essence it did.
Now, sir, I say that in that reply the minister misled the house. And immediately, so there will be no indication on my part to be unfair to the minister, I say to him I am sure he did not do it willingly because, knowing the minister as I have for years, that is not his method of approach to a question. But none the less that statement made by the minister is a misleading statement, because these are not the facts as I have ascertained from the report of the international joint commission.
What are the effects of the 1,000 c.f.s diversion out of the great lakes, as found by the international joint commission? I hold in my hand an interim report made to the international joint commission by the international lake Ontario board of engineers on this whole matter. This report is dated June 14, 1955. The purpose of the report is outlined at page 2, and I read:
The purpose of this interim report is to determine the effect on the levels of lake Ontario of 1,000 cubic feet per second increase in diversion out of lake Michigan at Chicago for a period of three years. The consequent effect of the lowering of lake Ontario upon navigation in lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence river and upon the generation of hydroelectric power at Niagara and in the St.

Lawrence river are also determined on the assumption that the three-year period of increase in diversions would commence on July 1, 1955.
Now, what are the tacts? According to this report, if this diversion were to take place there would be a maximum reduction instage of lake levels in lakes Michigan and Huron of .05 feet; lake Erie, .03 feet; and lake Ontario, .03 feet. In so far as navigation is concerned the reduction in levels in inches would be at Montreal harbour, three-eighths of an inch; in lake St. Louis, one quarter of an inch; in the harbours on lake Ontario, three-eighths of an inch; and in the harbours of other lakes such as Michigan and Huron, five-eighths of an inch.
This report also goes on to deal with the effect of the diversion in so far as power development in the downstream areas of the river is concerned. In the St. Lawrence river plants it is stated that reduction in flows of the St. Lawrence river, because of this 1,000 c.f.s. increase in Chicago diversion for three years, would reduce the water available to the plants now under construction at Barnhart island and the existing Cedars and Beauharnois plants, and the proposed addition to the Beauharnois plant and any proposed plants which may be constructed in the Lachine rapids section. Then the document concludes that the total energy losses at the Beauharnois, Cedars and Lachine plants will be in the neighbourhood of 86,600,000 kilowatt hours. Later on in the report, at page 12, it is said:
The total computed loss in energy at the above plants is 420 million kilowatt hours. Of this amount only 276 million kilowatt hours would be lost at existing plants and plants either under construction or actually scheduled for construction.
I should like to pause here for a moment to say this. While the bill will help to solve the sewage and drainage problem at Chicago, there is no justification for taking such an amount of water out of the great lakes basin, and it cannot be justified by any stretch of the imagination because it is not right from a moral standpoint. The waters belong to all the citizens of the great lakes, and if this is authorized then another additional amount will be sought by the Chicago drainage commission.
Perhaps the minister does not know, but it is a fact that at one stage the Chicago sanitary commission sought to get an additional amount of great lakes water in order to develop hydroelectric power in the Chicago area. That has been stated already before the rivers and harbours committee in the United States, where it has been said that the real motive behind this demand for increased diversion, according to the great
The Address-Mr. Chevrier lakes harbour association which gave evidence before that committee, is the desire on the part of the sanitary district of Chicago to obtain additional hydroelectric power to be developed by the facilities they own and operate, namely the hydroelectric project at Lockport, Illinois. In 1948 the assistant chief engineer of the sanitary district commission asserted that increased diversion could double the power output at the Lock-port plant of the sanitary district, and in 1947 the suggestion was made that increased diversion of water was needed for the development of atomic power because of the establishment of the Argonne laboratory on the banks of the sanitary district canal some 20 miles southwest of Chicago. Then in 1950 an appeal was made to President Truman to obtain additional diversion in order to obtain additional hydroelectric power during the coal strike.
Therefore it appears from those statements which are public and can be read by the minister, that the Chicago sanitary district is interested in obtaining additional diversion for power purposes.
The minister referred to an aide memoire which he tabled and which contained a protest against the possible diversion. I have obtained this aide memoire, which was printed as an appendix to Hansard; and while I am unable to find in this the kind of protest I would like to see, what I would like to bring to the attention of the minister is this. On page 2 of the aide memoire which has been given to me, while there is some general reference to the fact that it is assumed by the United States administration the diversion will have a detrimental effect on navigation and hydroelectric power generation in both countries, the reasons are not set out therein. In the concluding paragraph there is set out in some detail what the effect of this diversion will be on upriver interests, on lake levels in the upper regions of the lakes and on the international section, but not one word is said about downriver interests, and it is against this that I rise to protest today. I should like to quote what is said in the aide memoire.
However, if it were possible to offset part of the effects of the Chicago diversion by inflows from the Albany basin in Canada it would be equitable that an equivalent amount of water should remain available for use in hydroelectric power generation by the Ontario interests at St. Mary's falls, Niagara falls and in the international section of the St. Lawrence river until the effects of the proposed temporary diversion will have ceased to be felt in the great lakes system.
It is there that it seems to me that the aide memoire is deficient. It seems to me that there is no protest in the aide memoire

The Address-Mr. Chevrier about what will happen or is likely to happen to power development at Beau-harnois, at Lachine, at Cedars. I noticed in the press this morning that the minister of hydraulic resources, of the province of Quebec, indicates that there will soon be a development of hydroelectric power at Lachine. I welcome that announcement. I think it is all to the good. But if because of the 1,000 c.f.s. sought to be taken out of the great lakes over a period of three years that power development is affected below there should be the strongest protest on the part of the government.
There is also nothing in the note having to do with the water levels at the port of Montreal. If anything is done in the upstream end of the lakes that affects water levels at Montreal, navigation may be seriously affected. What is going to be the effect of the lowering by three-eights of an inch at the port of Montreal and the loss of these many millions of kilowatt hours that I mentioned earlier? I am not an electrical engineer and am not in a position to say. All I can say is that experts say that it is serious. Those who have knowledge of the matter in the United States have stated before a public committee there that it is the intention of the Chicago sanitary district authorities, if additional waters can be diverted from the great lakes, to develop power in that area. It seems to me that it would be unconscionable if water were taken from the great lakes for the development of power in that region.
Then there is no protest against the new bill itself, and that is what prompted me to say a moment ago that the minister had misled the house. There is no protest against bill No. 1. No protest has been launched against this particular bill. While a protest was launched against an anterior bill, which to my mind is a very weak protest, there has not been launched against this bill the kind of protest I should like to see and the kind of protest that I am sure the citizens of Canada want to see.
This is not a new problem. It is one which has attracted the attention of the country before. It is an old question that comes up from time to time, and Canada must be on its guard continually so that our rights with regard to the development of power in the international section as well as of navigation in the St. Lawrence will be protected.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to remind you that last Friday, in this house, the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) expressed his opinion about the actual contradictions with regard to the dispute between the C.B.C. and the

radio and television producers. However, since Friday, the situation has been deteriorating instead of improving. The right hon. Prime Minister recalled, in the course of the meeting, that his predecessor himself had already been blamed for intervening in C.B.C. affairs. He went on to say that it was not his intention to intervene in this dispute for fear of laying himself open to the same criticism.
This argument of the Prime Minister's is surely unacceptable. It is but a pretext used,
I think, in an effort to justify the incomprehensible stand taken by the government. We of the opposition have been asking every day, from the beginning of this session, through our questions to the Minister of Labour and to the Minister of National Revenue, to intervene in this dispute and to offer their good offices to both parties. In fact, we thought there was no reason why the government should not intervene within the terms of section 56(1) of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
Nobody could seriously claim that the government would exert undue influence by taking advantage of powers conferred upon it by this section of the act; on the contrary, it would only be doing its duty. So far, it has obstinately refused, without any good reason, to perform its duty. It seems to me that such an intervention would have been useful, and could have been of some help to the parties concerned who, at that time, were still in communication with each other. It would therefore have been possible to settle this dispute.

As far as we are concerned, we shall not permit the government to justify its lack of action by specious arguments like those put forward by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of National Revenue, since we consider that this dispute is very important. In fact, it might involve serious consequences, not only for the artists themselves, but for all those who are directly involved in that strike and, besides, for the whole future of the C.B.C. French network.
According to yesterday's papers, Mr. Speaker, C.B.C. officials are reported to have stated they were prepared to start over from scratch, rather than resume negotiations which they themselves had broken off with the producers. I submit that even if the C.B.C. officials wish to take this autocratic attitude, the people of Canada, who are paying the operating costs of the C.B.C. and who are interested in the French network, are not prepared to start again from scratch. I refer to responsibility either with respect to what they did before they were dismissed from office or indeed any responsibility whatsoever with respect to suggesting what might be done now by way of dealing with the situation.
I know the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and his colleagues are annoyed when we remind them of it but it is something of which they require to be reminded. The Leader of the Opposition showed his annoyance in his reference to a speech that I delivered to the young Conservatives on January 10. But we take the view that the country should be reminded of where the responsibility for the situation properly lies. We do not say and never have said-and I did not say it in that speech-that the Liberal government deliberately created the recession. No one goes so far as that. But I said -and I repeat it-that when we took office in June of 1957 we found as our chief inheritance the recession which had started while my hon. friends opposite were in power.

We do not and never have criticized the opposition when they stick to facts. We do not resent its criticism when it is based on facts and particularly when it is constructive. We ourselves do not deny the situation with which the country is confronted. It deserves and is receiving the serious attention of this government. We admit it is serious and do not criticize the opposition for pointing out its seriousness. We do, however, criticize our hon. friends opposite for trying to pretend that the situation is worse than it is and for putting on the record inventions which are passed by the name of statistics and thus presenting an inaccurate and exaggerated case. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the fact that my hon. friends are driven to the resort of using figures and analyses which are not accurate, and which I must say it is difficult for me to believe they did not know were not accurate, provides a pretty accurate measure of the real seriousness with which they themselves regard the situation. The fact that in discussing it they are driven to exaggeration to make a case at all shows that they themselves realize the situation is not as bad as they are trying to make out.

But the Leader of the Opposition is just an amateur in this field, as we shall see by comparing the inaccuracy of his statistics with those of the hon. member for Essex East. This also must be said, that at least the Leader of the Opposition does not try to make out that someone else is responsible for the incorrect statistics that he puts on the record. He is big enough to claim his errors as his own. However, in the hon. gentleman from Essex East we have a most remarkable statistician. His is a practice born of long experience. He is perfectly at home among figures-so much so that he can use them with perfect ease in an attempt to prove that things are, which, in fact, are not. On a number of occasions in the speech he made in this house on January 22 we have evidence of that. This is the serious criticism which I make of the hon. gentleman: not only that he is inaccurate-because we can all be inaccurate, though not quite as inaccurate as the hon. gentleman-but that he has attempted to attribute his inaccuracies to the dominion bureau of statistics.

I must say, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you will have shared this thought with me, that after the Liberal leadership convention of a year ago we had all imagined that the hatchet was buried, that rivalries were discontinued and that all was sweetness and harmony in the Liberal camp. But now we find that is not so because apparently the hon. member for Essex East is determined not to be outdone by his leader either in the scope or the size of his inaccuracies or in the sources of his information. As I have said, the Leader of the Opposition made no attempt to suggest that his statistics were other than his own, inaccurate though they were. The hon. member for Essex East, however, not content merely with inaccuracy, has sought to give his statistics an authority which they do not in fact possess by attributing them to the dominion bureau of statistics, thus seeking to outdo his leader.
It is not difficult to find a number of examples in the speech which the hon. gentleman made on January 22. He was criticizing the Prime Minister for a statement he had made that in the year just ended Canadians had worked more, earned more, spent more and saved more than in any comparable year in the history of this country, a statement which in virtually every particular, as a general statement, is true. The hon. gentleman did not wish to accept it. He did not wish to accept the truth of anything which the Prime Minister had said, because he knew it would not fit in with the propaganda which the Liberals were trying to sell in the country. Accordingly, he tried to show that the statement was not true in a number of particulars. Here is one example of what he did. The hon. gentleman said, referring to the Prime Minister, as reported in Hansard on page 181:
Then the hon. gentleman made the statement that Canadians spent more. Let us see what the dominion bureau of statistics itself has to say about this:
"It may be noted that on a per capita basis consumer purchases in real terms showed a year to year decline in all categories of expenditure in the first nine months of 1958."
Then, missing some of the following sentences, he says:
The Prime Minister, with these figures of the dominion bureau as my authority, is consequently proven wrong again.
Here we have a very odd piece of statistical reasoning on the part of the hon. gentleman. The Prime Minister in his statement referred to spending-general spending-when he said that Canadians spent more. In seeking to refute that statement the hon. member for Essex East has made a selective quotation from the dominion bureau of statistics dealing exclusively with consumer spending and, having found there one sentence referring to a

decline in consumer spending, he says: "Therefore, on the basis of the dominion bureau of statistics, the Prime Minister is wrong."
Let us see what the dominion bureau of statistics did actually say. I have the document in front of me. The hon. gentleman from Essex East was very coy the other day; he would not give us any page references when we asked him for them, but I have the source of his information-the chart at the top of page 6 dealing with percentage changes in expenditure by value, volume and price. This shows that gross national expenditure increased in the nine months reviewed in 1958 as compared with the nine months under review in 1957 in all three categories of value, volume and price.
The hon. gentleman must therefore admit that this shows clearly that the Prime Minister's statement was perfectly accurate and that his attempt to prove otherwise, and the quotation he used, was one of the most artificially selective of any I have heard used in this house for such a purpose. Then, carried away by his apparent success in this one attempt, the hon. gentleman persisted several stages further in his statistical magic. On the occasion I have just cited he did use the actual words of the dominion bureau of statistics, and attributed them accurately to the bureau. However, carried away by his apparent success he then proceeded to work up his own facts and attribute them to the dominion bureau. Let us look at an example, because this is really an extraordinary piece of statistical manoeuvering on the part of the hon. gentleman. He attacked the Prime Minister for an alleged inaccuracy in connection with a statement he made that Canadians earned more, and then the hon. gentleman says this-and I am quoting from the bottom of page 180 and the top of page 181- in an attempt to prove the Prime Minister wrong or, rather, to convince the house that the Prime Minister was wrong:
