We inherited the recession in June of 1957. Within a matter of months we had put $150 million into housing and we are still continuing to put money into housing. Within a matter of a few more months we had made considerable cuts in taxes. Within a matter of months we had substantially increased welfare payments. At the first opportunity to present a full budget we budgeted deliberately for a deficit. We have instituted and are continuing these and other work-providing programs. In addition to the housing and public works expenditures, which are continuing, there are the special winter works program started this year and the renewal of the northern affairs program of expenditure and work in the parks which was started last winter. We took the 1957 economic outlook report to heart although the Liberals had ignored it.

The Address-Mr. Fulton the best estimate that we can produce. Some 36,750 national housing loans were taken up during 1958. The total of federal funds made available under these loans was $375 million. It is estimated that these federal housing loans provided around 92,000 man years of employment. This impressive total is made up of about 46,000 man years of on-site labour and the same amount of off-site labour. This, of course, relates only to the federal funds made available and does not take into account the tremendous flow of private mortgage funds that has been going into housing construction under the stimulation of the policies of my colleague, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green). It has been estimated that the total number of men employed in the housing program generally is certainly, at a conservative estimate, at least 600,000.
In addition to housing loans, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been engaged in the construction of public housing and other buildings. The expenditure involved in these has amounted to over $30 million.
Then, other departments responsible for construction programs include the Department of Transport, and their program includes the development and maintenance of airports, the construction and maintenance of harbours, the St. Lawrence seaway and large expenditures by such crown corporations as the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines. Well over $400 million of federal government expenditures have been made on works projects in this field during 1958. It is estimated that at least 80,000 man-years of employment, including both on-site and off-site work have resulted from these expenditures.
With respect to the Department of Public Works, it is estimated that all their normal expenditures during the year 1958 have meant employment over the course of a year for at least another 25,000 men, on-site and off-site. These statistics are in terms of man-years, Mr. Speaker, and this is an impressive total.
Then, the northern affairs and national resources program continued from last winter, it is estimated is providing employment on a continuous basis for at least 3,000 men to date. In so far as the special municipal winter works program is concerned, the latest estimate which my colleague the Minister of Labour has furnished me shows that it is expected for Canada as a whole there will be 1,086,895 man-days of work provided by that program to be initiated between December 1 and April 1.

This is the first instalment of the government's attempt to implement that promise.

have never followed John, but on this one occasion in the throne speech I am following Dave. I must admit this has been a rather amusing session, with so many statistics flying around. I think it is understandable why so many people are a little confused at the moment. They do not know whether the figures are lying or the liars are figuring. It is one or the other.
It is quite evident, also, that there has been a lot of political name-calling during this session in attempts to place responsibility. This reminds me of the story of two men who went out on a bender. It was a real drunk. When they woke up the next morning they found themselves in bed with a corpse between them. Fearing the consequences, they both dashed to the police station and blamed the other for homicide which was, of course, of no interest to the corpse at all. Basically, this is what has been going on since this house met, especially on the question of unemployment and right now the problem of the producers of the C.B.C.
Basically, we are not going to solve anything by even trying to find out who was responsible. The point is that there are certain circumstances extant in this country which require to be handled, and our responsibility, irrespective of party, government or opposition, is not to damn each other so much for the evils of the past, but to see if we cannot be good right now and in the future. I was interested in all the statistics put forward by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and all the others. But a man or a woman who is unemployed or on strike or locked out is not a statistic. He or she is a human being in need of something being done about their problem. I was most interested in the closing remarks of the Minister of Justice when he dealt once again, almost word for word, with the statement the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made in the campaign of last year. The Prime Minister said that if he were elected no one would go without or suffer in this country.
The reason why we have to get up and speak on these matters so often, and perhaps be so repetitious, is that people are suffering and are hungry in Canada and the government has not done anything about that. Admittedly you can bring forth all these figures showing increased emloyment and increased income. Of course, this country is not static; it is growing. People are being born every day. People are going into the employment field every day. Immigrants are coming in, or they have been, by the thousands. We have what almost looks like

a paradox but is not, and that is employment going up at the same time as unemployment is going up. Of course, we are happy about the increase in employment.
What we want to know is what you are going to do about your promises to those who are unemployed. You admit that there are 749,000 who are asking for employment. Whether it is 100,000 or 749,000 I ask what about those who need that work? Last May- I have the actual dates here, May 12 of last year, May 28, July 9, July 12 of last year- I have all the Hansard quotes here-the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) said-because they must have had some recognition of the dangers of unemployment and suffering this winter and spring -that they would introduce changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. They never did and we are still waiting for those changes.
But because they neglected their responsibilities, because they did not fulfil their promise made on all the dates I have given you last year, Mr. Speaker, there are thousands upon thousands in this country who are no longer eligible for unemployment insurance, nor can they get work. The government say they take care of them. They go on welfare. What is welfare? In one of our provinces, it is about half of the amount they would receive were they eligible for unemployment insurance. Nobody on unemployment insurance is living in the lap of luxury. What do you do about those who have to depend upon welfare? I say this to the government. Why sit back so smug and holy about the fact that you are paying 50 per cent of starvation sustenance for those people who, because of your negligence, are not now covered by unemployment insurance and who have not jobs?

Time after time at this session the Prime Minister has appealed for co-operation. Let me say this to the hon. members on the government side of the house. As far as Vancouver is concerned, he has offers of co-operation right down the line from the trades and labour council, unemployment committees and so on. Before this house was called together elected members of all parties were called in to discuss the situation. The parks commissioners of Vancouver called in the elected members to talk over their problems. The Vancouver city council called in the representatives to talk over the situation and the problems. There was co-operation on the labour level, on the parks committee level and the municipal level, recognizing that the solution does not lie with one level of government but that because the federal government is the senior government, it is from there that the major direction and the major aid will have to come.
The other members from the city of Vancouver in this house can tell you, Mr. Speaker, as I do, that the city of Vancouver said this: If you give us a little bit more progressive aid, not just half the cost of labour on the particular works but half the cost, then within four weeks we will have project after project under way. I am convinced that if this government, instead of

The Address-Mr. Winch trying to allocate blame and say "It is not our fault", would recognize the problem and come forward with some emergency measures in the way of municipal assistance, special welfare assistance and change in the Unemployment Insurance Act so as to make the unemployed eligible for something as of right and not charity, they would get a spontaneous acceptance from the people and from the various levels of government. I can say that at least for the province I know best, namely the province of British Columbia.
When we speak of unemployment solutions, naturally we must think of production and trade. It has been somewhat of a disappointment to us in this group that so little has been said on the cabinet level as to Canada's position in world trade, the problems which we face in that area and just how we are going to meet the situation.
I was most pleased to read in the Globe and Mail of this morning a report under dateline of Washington, January 26, as follows:
Canadian Justice Minister Fulton is visiting his opposite number here this week for discussions on how to avoid in the future what Canadians consider attempts by Washington to make U.S. laws rather than Canadian laws applicable to Canada.
I know we certainly want to wish the minister well on that trip but I think that now is the time to emphasize how emphatic he must be when he visits Washington. There is not only a growing fear but a growing understanding that irrespective of what must have been a beautiful talk between the Prime Minister and President Eisenhower last year and the indications given to us that this problem of United States domination of Canadian companies was going to cease, that was just a lot of tommyrot because the situation has definitely not improved. As a matter of fact, it has worsened.
Not only do I take the position-and I do it personally, of course, from my reading-that nothing has been done whatsoever about the matter but evidence is now forthcoming to demonstrate that we are even more than ever dominated by the United States with respect to our goods produced in Canada, and to companies which are subsidiaries to those in the United States. There is no need to repeat what we all know of the motor car incident of last year with regard to sales to the peoples' republic of China. That was the first indication. Perhaps not too much emphasis should be placed on it but it is worthy of note. We receive information that Alcan, from the headquarters in Montreal, honestly admit that they turned down a sale to China at the same time they were laying off 620 men because of their fear of repercussions in their major markets in the United States. But the matter goes even beyond that.

I have a friend who is well known as a member of the bar association in Ontario and who last fall made a visit to Chungking. Whilst he was in Chungking he was entertained by the president of the chamber of commerce there and he watched freight being unloaded by hand from hundreds of junks on the waterfront. The president of the chamber of commerce told him that they were going to initiate plans to utilize conveyor belts for this unloading. Our esteemed friend from Canada informed the president of the chamber of commerce in Chungking that Canada produced conveyor belting of the highest quality, something which all hon. members know is true. When my friend returned to Canada or shortly thereafter he happened to visit the B. F. Goodrich plant. They made inquiries about his trip to China, being interested, and he told them about this opportunity of selling belting to Chungking. They were interested. But do you know what happened? May I also extend a word of welcome to those members who have joined us in the house since the beginning of this session. I hope their stay in parliament will be a long and successful one.
I should like to turn now to the speech from the throne which contains a list of policies and actions to be approved by the House of Commons which I think are going to be of great benefit to Canada in the days to come. Much has been said in this debate so far on the subject of unemployment. Much has been said by the opposition which would lead us to believe that the country is on the verge of collapse economically. I wish the people of Canada could observe the faces of the opposition; how great a look of disappointment is registered thereon when the steady improvement in our economy is noted, and how great a look of delight, almost to the point of rapture, overcomes them when unemployment figures are quoted.

I do not propose to go into the figures again. They are all on record. No one denies that we have unemployment in Canada. No one denies that last winter the figures were higher than usual. No one can deny that the figures this winter are improving all the time as the result of government action, but we do and should deny that the picture in Canada is as bad as it is painted by the opposition. The picture which the opposition paints is not designed to suggest ways and means of improving the situation but is designed to spread fear and panic in the hearts and minds of the people of Canada.
What have the members of the opposition to offer by way of suggestion? Nothing. They criticize but do not come up with any ideas of their own. The fact of the matter is that they have no ideas, because everything has been done by this government which can be done within the realm of practicality and common sense. The actions which this government took in national housing, in tax reductions, in increased social security benefits, in increased unemployment insurance benefits, in a program of public works and in easing credit prevented the situation from being a great deal worse than it was and have contributed in large part to the recovery which we are experiencing today.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) goes back to 1957 and tries to explain what he would have done had he still been in power. The measures which he suggests would have been too late. The former government had its opportunity in early 1957 to forestall a recession and to alleviate its effects. They had the information and the advice of the economic experts upon which to make a decision. They had two courses to follow and they chose the wrong one. They chose to fight inflation and ignored the warning signs of recession and unemployment. When the Leader of the Opposition says what he would have done had he remained in power I can only say that his hindsight and that of his colleagues is obviously a great deal better than their foresight.
The truth of the matter is that when the present government assumed office in 1957 they inherited a multitude of problems created by the Liberal administration. Had these problems not been created the Liberals would not have been turned out of office. The people of Canada lost confidence in them and expressed themselves at the polls by turning them out. For the Leader of the Opposition to expect this government to have dealt with the accumulation of decisions and have solved the multitude of problems which were left to it at that time in the short space
The Address-Mr. Thompson of 19 months is the same as to expect someone to unravel a tangled skein of yarn in a matter of seconds. He could not do it and neither could anyone else.
Many references have been made to the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) that as long as he is Prime Minister no one will suffer from unemployment. As usual, this statement has been misinterpreted by the opposition to have a meaning different from that which the Prime Minister intended. It is interpreted as a guarantee of 100 per cent employment, but any sensible person knows that that is not possible. What the Prime Minister obviously meant to any reasonable person is that he would emphasize and give priority to the fight against unemployment and do everything reasonable and practical to reduce unemployment and to alleviate the hardships of those who might be affected. This he has done and is doing.
In closing my remarks on this subject, Mr. Speaker, I, like the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith), would like to say with what interest I listened to the answers given to questions by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) at the press conference last week. His only answer was that the duty of the opposition is to criticize the policies and actions of the government. I must say that I was at a loss to know whether he had some ideas up his sleeve which he was just keeping to himself or whether he had no ideas at all and was just trying to cover up. As the time passed by I became inclined to the latter view.
Certainly, if the hon. member for Essex East has any ideas at all it is his duty to bring them before this house for consideration. The government has the responsibility to initiate whatever measures are deemed necessary, but every member has the duty to disclose any ideas which he might have to further the best interests of his country. If the opposition proposes to do nothing from now on except to criticize and not offer any alternative ideas, then I wish them good luck because I think they are going to be in opposition for a long time. I do not think that the people of Canada will allow any group to form a government which does not offer a reasonable and better alternative to the government of the day.

added that this picture was contrary to the facts and with his customary self-complacency, stated that the Leader of the Opposition was not equal to his responsibilities as a leader. In fact the Prime Minister said, about the Leader of the Opposition:
"He is not living up to his responsibilities at this time when the world situation is difficult and distressing".
And later on:
"When we think of the difficulties that face the free world in the form of an economic onslaught."
In the same breath he says that the Leader of the Opposition is wrong in blackening Canada's reputation and right afterwards he tells the Leader of the Opposition: "You were perfectly right."

There were 133,000 unemployed in December 1952, 193,000 in 1953, 252,000 in 1954, 200,000 in 1955, 188,000 in 1956, while in 1957, when our good friends came to power, there were 392,000. In 1958, they numbered 440,000.

They used to wail and lament, Mr. Speaker, and they acted like calamity howlers. Were they being truthful at that time? No, and yet now they criticize us for telling people the truth. Just recently the producers' strike on the French network of the C.B.C. raised a problem. Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak tonight, I would like to welcome the hon. members for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman), for Springfield (Mr. Slogan) who sit with us for the first time and for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer).

The Address-Mr. Campeau
Before recess this afternoon, I had pointed out that we were proud of the national development program mentioned in the speech from the throne, because it expresses a will to expand similar to the one shown by the fathers of confederation when they wanted, almost a century ago, to make a Canada "a mari usque ad mare". In our opinion, it is in this respect that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has shown his profound understanding of Canada's basic mission as a nation, within the framework of confederation, by offering to all Canadians an opportunity to build by practical stages a Canada by and for all Canadians closely united in a development of which they are willing to pay the price in order that its immense benefits may be secured both for themselves and for their children. We are grateful to the right hon. Prime Minister for devoting all his energy to the realization of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's vision: "The twentieth century belongs to Canada".
Mr. Speaker, in connection with this national development policy based on the functional development of natural resources, I would like to stress the importance of physical and human capital as represented by urban development the most typical expression of which is the constituency of St. James.
The development of cities in Canada has been so rapid that it is now the source of a problem facing the whole Canadian people. More than 65 per cent of the Canadian population now live in the cities, towns or villages, and more than 36 per cent in major metropolitan areas. The Gordon commission foresees that during the next 25 years the urban population will reach 80 per cent of the total Canadian population. This urban expansion will affect more than 2,000 square miles of land and require an extra capital outlay of $4,100 billion for housing, educational and other institutions as well as municipal works.
Obviously this urban expansion requires a concentrated effort to achieve at all levels of government an effective co-ordination of the activities aiming at solving those urban problems which are more and more numerous, important and urgent.
More and more, public works undertaken by the federal government play a necessarily paramount role in the urban development throughout this country.
A realistic approach shows that it is expedient, indeed necessary, that federal

The Address-Mr. Campeau activities be organized so as to tie in with local and regional town planning. In the matter of housing, slum clearance, government buildings and other similar projects, individual projects can and should be mapped out so as to fit in the master plans worked out by the municipalities. Many public works, thus thought out and implemented, could meet federal needs while replacing or at least fitting in the local projects. This procedure could bring to the municipalities in most cases a much more substantial help than grants without giving rise to any constitutional issues. Thus local and regional town planning would be furthered as it has never been in the past.
It can be said without exaggeration that it would be proper to initiate research at the federal government level, in order to establish the relationship that could exist between federal projects on the one hand and municipal projects on the other, as foreseen in the planning schemes of the municipalities. These projects could replace or complete one another in the best interests of the municipalities.
It therefore appears essential and urgent that the national development program be drawn up in such a way as to provide positive help for urban development throughout the country, in fields where federal activity is already intense, such for example as those of natural resources, public works, transportation and communications, and of low cost and low rental housing. Such co-ordination must be achieved at the federal level in order to give practical aid to municipalities that are experiencing growing pains.
As an illustration, Mr. Speaker, may I refer to the constituency of St. James, in the context of the Montreal area.
The National Housing Act, and the generous amounts placed at the disposal of builders in the last few months, thanks to the Conservative government, give hopes for a substantial improvement of housing conditions in the very heart of Montreal.
The example set by the Jeanne Mance home building project will certainly be followed by other similar schemes for slum clearance and low rental family dwellings. I wish to assure my constituents of St. James that we will spare no efforts to ensure that the renovation initiated in our constituency will be pursued actively in the future. At this point, I wish to thank my colleague, the

hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade) who shared my efforts to secure for the eastern portion of the centre of the city, the benefits of the National Housing Act, and thus to bring forth in the eastern part of the city a development of real estate comparable to that enjoyed by the western portion of centre town.
The harbour is constantly improving and already the wharves are spreading towards the east of the island of Montreal, on the north shore while on the south shore, expansion projects are getting under way in the area of Varennes, Vercheres and Contrecoeur. We have reason to believe that, in the near future, there will be a bridge or a tunnel across Ste. Therese island to connect the harbour developments of the north shore with those of the south shore and to facilitate trading between both shores, while providing an easy access for the working population of the eastern part of the island of Montreal, to this colossal industry which is growing on the south shore and which needs this supply of labour to develop adequately.
The harbour development will require traffic and parking facilities that will have to be integrated with those of the city of Montreal. The harbour's commercial traffic already requires a speedway that could be connected with the multi-lane highway project recommended by the city of Montreal along the harbour, from Place Royale to Bonsecours church, and even further towards the extreme east.
Parking facilities urgently needed at the harbour, both for its employees and visitors who go there on business, could be developed in such a way as to meet on occasion the needs of neighbouring industries.
In the very near future, the development of jet planes will require a decentralization of airport services in Dorval. Consideration should be given right away to providing a functional area to this end, in view of the fact that the urban development of Montreal is rapidly reducing to nothing the great vacant spaces. In view of the intensive industrial development which is taking place in the Vercheres, Varennes and Contrecoeur area, the territory where Ste. Therese island is located should be seriously examined with a view to maintaining and intensifying the residential industrial and harbour development of that expanding area.
The utilization of railway rights of way for public transportation purposes would help to

solve rapidly a major problem facing the economic life of Montreal, and at the same time it would lighten the heavy burden of commuters' services provided by railway companies. The advantage of such a solution would be to fully utilize a capital already invested and to provide the public transportation problem with a solution which would certainly be the most economical and especially the most rapid.
Finally, the construction of public buildings, if their location is integrated in the overall city plan, is a substantial renovating factor, and a creator of real estate increment value which is of benefit to the whole area concerned. We believe that due to the intensive development of the Montreal area, a new concentration of federal services will become advisable in the near future. It would be logical to consider, to this end, the eastern part of central Montreal which would be very convenient for the setting up of an administrative centre. Such a measure, developed in accordance with a functional town-planning concept, would help eradicate slum areas, would provide a radical element of renovation and would encourage, on the part of private enterprise, large scale programs to the advantage of the whole eastern part of the island of Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, in closing my remarks, I speak on behalf of the citizens of St. James constituency in expressing our confidence in the future of Montreal, of the province of Quebec and of Canada.
We are not afraid of recessions, regressions and inflation. We do not allow ourselves to be frightened more than necessary by the prophets of doom who unconsciously interfere with the good name of their own national institutions. We are not happy with unemployment, but we don't enjoy either the abstract calculations of so-called experts who are ready to oiler solutions to any problem, remedies unable to withstand the dire laws of reality.

The Address-Mr. Tucker and Cartier, we want to set in the stone, brick and concrete, for the benefit of the following generations, an unlimited vision of the future of Canada.

We have been waiting for months for the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to make a statement on the McNair report respecting term 29 and Tories and Liberals alike in Newfoundland are expecting an upward revision based on this report. In term 29 of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada there is written the consummation of the union of Newfoundland with Canada, the grand finale of the linking of two British dominions, the dominion of Newfoundland with the dominion of Canada, and as in the marriage ceremony one and one when joined together make one. So we now have one great dominion, the great dominion of Canada which stretches from the Pacific to the Atlantic. As it is said that the twentieth century belongs to Canada, Canada is now called upon to act generously to her newly adopted child at a time when the ruling

Newfoundland will be far behind even the maritimes until the federal government of Canada meets its obligations to the latest adopted member of the Canadian family. reaching their decision. Because of the failure of the fishery, a large majority of the fishermen in Newfoundland, through no fault of their own, did not get enough stamps to get unemployment insurance. We had in the Newfoundland cod fishery the worst crop failure in Canada. All Liberal members from Newfoundland join in strong representations to the Prime Minister that something should be done for these fishermen, something comparable with what the government did for the farmers in the west. All Newfoundland fishermen were disappointed when on Tuesday, January 20, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) told us that nothing could be done for our fishermen. On page 78 of Hansard for that date there was a supplementary question asked of the minister by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) as follows:
Did I understand the minister to say consideration is no longer being given to a reduction in the number of stamps required by fishermen for unemployment insurance?
The minister answered as follows:
I said, sir, no consideration is being given to reducing the 15 stamps that are required for seasonal benefits at the moment, and that includes everyone.
Newfoundland fishermen, work hard and long, from daylight to sunset. They worked a sufficient number of hours but they did not get enough fish to enable them to obtain sufficient stamps to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. This regulation is just not fair to our Newfoundland fishermen. fish produced than in any year on record. As a matter of fact, we had a decrease of 40 per cent in lightly salted fish and 35 per cent in heavily salted fish.
In addition to our salt fish industry we annually export to the United States of America approximately 60 million pounds of fresh frozen fish. In 1958 there were approximately 450 million pounds of fish caught, 100 million pounds less than in the previous year. A shortage of bait, the failure of the trawl and trap fisheries and stormy weather were amongst the -chief factors for the failure of the shore fisheries. The federal department has taken steps to have mobile bait units placed in a few fishing settlements. I urge the government to send more to Newfoundland because I am convinced that while these depots will not solve the main difficulties they will go a long way toward helping the fishermen.
At the present time it looks as if there will be more men prosecuting the fishery in 1959 than there have been for a number of years. I sincerely hope that their efforts will be amply repaid. For more than 100 years the cod trap, hook and line and trawls have been the methods of shore fishing in Newfoundland. We have now approximately 70,500 fishermen in 1,300 settlements along our 6,000 miles of rugged but picturesque coastline. It can be seen, therefore, that the fisheries still are, as they have been, one of our main industries and every effort should be made by this government to see that all measures are taken to protect and assist this most important industry which can and should be further developed. When we consider the nature of the inshore fishing, and the present system followed by our shore fishermen, we can see that salt fish will be produced mainly for many years to come.
I understand that for a number of years the building of fish stages has been under consideration, and recently the federal government approved of the construction of some 20 community fish stages in Newfoundland. It is estimated, I believe, the cost will be $500,000, and the sites selected are supposed to be in the areas most affected by the failure of the fishery in 1958. At the present time the fishermen have their own fish stages for landing their fish, their own storerooms for salting their fish and their own flakes for drying their fish. These community stages should be a great help in producing a more uniform quality of fish, and should enable our fishermen to operate more efficiently. I understand that two of these stages are to be built in the riding of Trinity-Conception in the near future. I hope that more will be built next year.
The Address-Mr. Tucker
I would strongly recommend that these community stages be erected in the late fall and early spring rather than during the winter because high seas and stormy weather make it practically impossible for the men to work and produce anything worth while for their efforts. Last year most of the bait that we had in our cold storage was sold to competitors, and we had to bring in bait.
Some 400,000 pounds of European squid were brought to Newfoundland. Steps should be taken to see that this does not happen again. Instead steps should be taken to see that all the cold storages are filled to capacity if and when bait of the species of caplin, squid, herring and mackerel are available. Reports of stocks should be presented weekly to the department concerned. In Newfoundland today we have another problem, namely that of our coastal fleet which is practically a thing of the past. I think the time is now opportune for giving assistance in the matter of the building of schooners of from 100 gross tons to 200 gross tons for this important purpose, especially when we consider the fact that most of our coastal boats are nigh ready for the scrap heap and are not being replaced and supplemented at a sufficient pace to keep up the poor service now in existence, let alone improve it.

Twenty-five miles of this is through the national park which is a federal responsibility. This leaves a distance of 542 miles to be built by the province of Newfoundland. Of this, 256 miles have already been built and are ready for paving. Thirty-five miles have been paved, leaving 286 miles to be built and a total of 508 miles to be paved.
The minister estimated the cost of building the highway would be $31,500,000 for the construction of 286 miles and $22,600,000 for the paving of 508 miles and $4,223,000 for the building or construction of 34 bridges making a grand total of $58,225,000 to be spent on roads. With the present agreement between the province and the federal government Newfoundland will have to spend $28,112,000. The minister further stated that Newfoundland has to build more miles of the trans-Canada highway per capita than any other province in Canada. He also said that when the present agreement expires in 1960 he feels a more realistic division of cost

should be agreed upon; otherwise the trans-Canada highway from St. John's to Vancouver will not be completed for at least another ten years.
I hope that the speech which I have just delivered will not have fallen on deaf ears but that the present government will give serious consideration to many of the problems of Newfoundland which because of many factors are unique. I should like to tell the government that we are not seeking something to which we are not entitled.
At this time I wish to repeat my leader's appeal to the government to conclude this debate immediately and proceed at once with legislation to deal with the unemployment problem. As long as the government persists in prolonging the debate and delaying action the Liberal party will take its part in the debate but we are ready to have the vote now and get on with the nation's business.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words must be of congratulation to the mover (Mr. Jorgenson) and the seconder (Mr. Fortin) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The hon. member for Provencher brought to the attention of this house in his masterful way the viewpoint, the problems and the aspirations of the western farmer. The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet in that beautiful French language expressed very clearly not only the wish but the need for complete national unity of all those ethnic groups that make up our nation. I should like to express the thought that on March 31, 1958 in the general election held on that day one of the most forward steps in national unity since confederation was taken by the good people of Quebec when they sent to this house 50 Conservative members of the 75 who were elected from "la belle" province.
I could not let this opportunity pass, Mr. Speaker, without saying a few words about your person. I have had the privilege of sitting in this house in the 23rd parliament and, of course, in the first session of the 24th parliament under your chairmanship. I have been deeply impressed as I know all hon. members have been by your fairness, your great knowledge of procedure and especially by your keen sense of humour. In this debate it is permissible for an hon. member to discuss his constituency. I should like to follow that precedent and for a part of the time at my disposal this evening discuss the constituency of York-Sunbury, New Brunswick, a beautiful part of a beautiful province. For the past 36 years York-Sunbury has had only four members in this house and I should like to pay my tribute to their service.
The Address-Mr. MacRae
For 19 years our representative was the Hon. R. B. Hanson, minister of trade and commerce in the government of the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett and later leader of the official opposition. For a period of five years it was represented by the Hon. W. G. Clark, later lieutenant-governor of our province. From 1945 to 1947, following his return from war service, our representative was the Hon. H. F. G. Bridges as minister of fisheries. It was a great loss not only to his party and to the government of the day but to the country as a whole when the life of this able young man was cut short in 1947. From 1947 to 1957 York-Sunbury was represented by the Hon. Milton F. Gregg, V.C., whose portfolio for much of that time was that of labour. These hon. gentlemen represented York-Sunbury well and I am happy to be able to have this opportunity to pay this tribute to them.
The city of Fredericton is the largest centre in my constituency. Founded by the United Empire Loyalists in 1884 it is the seat of government for the province of New Brunswick. It has grown rapidly in the past dozen years, a condition which we hope to see continue. Nearby is the cotton milling town of Marysville. I would like to pause for just a moment at this point to express the thanks of the people of Marysville to the government for legislation passed in the previous session, the so-called anti-dumping legislation, which has made it possible for the major industry in this town to continue and to prosper. The textile industry as everyone knows is highly competitive. The legislation to which I have referred provides some degree of protection against the dumping of foreign textiles on the Canadian market which have been forcing our textile mills out of production. One year ago in this small mill there were 110 men and women employed. Today 200 are employed.
Fredericton is on the trans-Canada highway. A beautiful new bridge known as the Princess Margaret bridge will be officially opened this summer. Nearby, too, is the dominion experimental farm which is a credit to the Department of Agriculture and the government service as a whole. Within a few weeks construction of a new administration and science laboratory is to be commenced there costing in the neighbourhood of $1,750,000. Fredericton has its own municipal airport. However, the great expansion of the area has made the present facilities inadequate. Representations have been made to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) about this and I would ask his full co-operation which I am sure will be forthcoming in
412	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. MacRae giving consideration to the legitimate requests which have been made by the city administration.
York-Sunbury also has other communities of some importance, the railway centre of MacAdam and the Minto coal mining area. I share with the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) the honour of representing the fine people in this area. I was deeply distressed as I am sure all hon. members of the house were to hear that there are to be temporary lay-offs in the Nova Scotian coal fields.
The employment picture in Minto has been brighter this winter than for several years past. And while I am discussing unemployment I might mention that I took the opportunity this afternoon to check the employment figures in my constituency and I found that there are 300 fewer people unemployed today than there were a year ago.
Now I should like to tell the house for a few moments about Camp Gagetown. Here in York-Sunbury and Royal is located what is considered to be one of the finest and most modern military installations in the world. The camp area contains over 500 square miles of the finest military training country in Canada, comprising training ranges, general manoeuver areas and localities for exercises for almost all types of warfare from jungle to mountain fighting. Secondly, there is the administration of the camp, with its more than 100 beautiful and functional buildings. Thirdly, and adjacent, is the married quarters where 2,000 homes provide service men and their families with excellent accommodation. Construction of this camp was begun in 1953 and it was officially opened on July 1, 1958 by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes).
Beside the camp, where there was formerly only a small village known as Oro-mocto, there is growing a new city under a federal-provincial planning committee. Presently stationed at Camp Gagetown is the third Canadian infantry brigade group, a formation well-officered, well-manned and well-trained, and containing over 3,000 of Canada's finest soldiers. Camp Gagetown has had a marked effect on the economy of our province. It cost in the neighbourhood of $100 million to build. The annual payroll of servicemen and civilians is around $15 million. One example of its effect on our economy is the fact that in its central heating plant alone up to 300 tons of New Brunswick coal is burned every day in the winter time.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to talk about the economic needs and aspirations of my province as a whole. During the past two
[Mr. MacRae. 1

years especially great strides have been made. The program of power development in the Atlantic provinces, which is part of the policy of this present government, is of vital importance. Without electric power readily available at reasonable cost industry cannot function. The bill passed in the twenty-third parliament to lend $30 million to New Brunswick for the Beechwood hydro development was hailed in all parts of the province. The assistance which was promised, and which will be given in due course, to promote thermal power development will be of inestimable value. I need hardly say that the equalization grants paid to New Brunswick and to the other Atlantic provinces have had a most beneficial effect on our economy.
Mr. Speaker, I would urge the government to give further consideration to the following measures to develop not only New Brunswick but the whole Atlantic area. First, federal capital assistance to develop our resources. Our region is rich in minerals and forests but without federal aid we cannot develop them to the advantage of our area and the rest of Canada. I was deeply interested, as I am sure all members from the maritimes were interested, in the particular clause from the speech from the throne which read as follows:
My government will continue in its economic policies to lay emphasis upon national development. My ministers believe that by the wise use of the resources with which nature has endowed this country, Canadians can achieve a continually rising standard of living. My government will therefore foster and encourage the proper development and use of these resources and the growth of efficient industry based upon them. Many projects for national development have already been put in hand; you will be asked to vote the supply necessary to continue these projects and to initiate others.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot have national development on its full scale unless every part of our nation is developed. There can be no second-class Canadians and there can be no second-class areas of Canada. I would urge our government to look towards the east. We in the maritimes, now as never before, require assistance on a grand scale to bring ourselves out of the financial doldrums in which we have found ourselves for nearly a century.
Our second request of the government is for a capital projects program which would provide federal assistance for provincial projects to enlarge the basic economy of our area. The Chignecto canal and the Prince Edward Island causeway are examples. We are proud, as all Canadians should be, of the magnificent St. Lawrence seaway, but one of the effects of the seaway could be to injure the great Atlantic all-year ports of Halifax and Saint John. We in the maritimes

also contributed to the building of the seaway. I would ask the government, through its appropriate minister, to press with vigour the investigation which is being conducted with regard to the Chignecto canal. We in the Atlantic provinces may again have to look to the sea for the shipment of the products of our region. The Chignecto canal should be of inestimable value from a transportation point of view.
Hon. members may remenber the former member for Westmorland making a very humorous suggestion-I think it was during the course of the twenty-third parliament- to the effect that both the canal project and the causeway project should be carried out at the same time by digging out the Chignecto canal and dumping the material into the strait to form the causeway. Unfortunately, the idea would not work.
Third, we would ask for a program of industrial decentralization. We note that as time goes on more and more industries are being concentrated in the central part of Canada, especially defence industries and crown corporations. We can well remember that during world war II very few defence industries were established in the maritime provinces. The minister of the Liberal government at that time made a statement in defence of this policy when he said: "After all, what would we do with them when the war is over?" In this day of nuclear warfare, dispersion is one of the basic principles of defence. We have the electric power and we can obtain more to turn the wheels of industry. We have the manpower-and it is good manpower-to staff the factories. All we need is a policy of decentralization which will locate those industries in the Atlantic region. I would ask our government to keep that in mind at all times.
Fourth, I would urge the government to implement a transportation policy which will provide the opportunity for our products to be carried to and sold in the markets of Canada at competitive prices. The recent increase in the freight rates of from 17 to 21 per cent was a crippling blow to us. There is an application pending for further increases which, if granted, could be the straw that could break the proverbial camel's back in our area. It is the long haul shippers of the Atlantic provinces who are hardest hit by the freight rate increase. With each increase it becomes harder for the Atlantic provinces to compete successfully in central Canadian markets. Each increase raises the price to both Atlantic region manufacturers and consumers of the goods and raw materials they import. A special committee of government is now studying this problem and legislation is
The Address-Mr. MacRae to be brought down at this session. I hope that the deliberations and the legislation will provide a solution, but no half way measures will serve here. Legislation will not be of help unless there is a formula to protect us from the ravages of future freight rate increases.
One of the most forward steps taken in the Atlantic area in the last few years to raise the standard of living in our region has been the creation of the Atlantic provinces economic council, usually referred to as APEC.
APEC was formed in September of 1954. Its whole purpose was the improvement of the economic status of the area. It cuts across all lines. It embodies all people in all walks of life. The only requirement of those who wish to belong to this organization is that they must want to really contribute to the growth of the Atlantic region. Some of the projects which they have successfully sponsored have been exhibitions of maritime products, area trade fairs and the opening of the Atlantic provinces office in London, England.
APEC is attempting to attract the interest of industry and trade bodies to the possibility of establishing in the Atlantic area branches, outlets and purchasing centres. Its main function at the moment is as a fact-finding organization and then to stimulate the people of the area into economic action on the basis of the facts that it makes available. A former president of APEC expresses it this way:
APEC's basic interest lies in a man with an idea, a government with a policy and an organization with a plan, all designed to produce economic betterment for the Atlantic region and for Canada as a nation.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, finally to discuss for a few moments an item in connection with our basic resource, namely our forests. New Brunswick, or most of its area, is covered with spruce and fir. I believe as an individual that we are not utilizing to its fullest extent the potential that is there. We know from experience what can happen when a resource is depleted through unwise use and exploitation. I had the opportunity recently of reading the brief presented by the Canadian lumbermen's association to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton). This body presented a number of extremely valuable recommendations, especially concerning research and I would urge the minister to have his officials thoroughly consider the recommendations of this association. While their proposals must of necessity be viewed from a national basis yet, as I said, because the forests of our province are its greatest asset, those proposals vitally affect us in New Brunswick-

The Address-Mr. Leduc
I have covered those points in connection with my constituency and my province which I wished to bring before the house at this time and in so doing have tried to emphasize the needs of the people whom I represent. May I sum up by saying that we believe- those of us who live in the Atlantic community-that we are entitled to the benefits of opportunity and security, which shall be no more, but shall certainly be no less, than all Canadians have the right to enjoy. I believe that this government, which has proven in fewer than two years to be one of the ablest administrations since confederation, will do everything in its power to see that this objective is attained.

Mr. Speaker, I followed closely and with great interest the speeches of the different members who spoke on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and I noticed that all of them have commended you for the impartial manner in which you preside over the debates of the house.
Mr. Speaker, not only do I offer you my most sincere congratulations, but I wish that the government, and particularly the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), would implement the election promise that was made to the people of Canada, that of appointing a permanent Speaker. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from a speech that the present Prime Minister made in Carman, Manitoba, on May 15, 1957, as reported in a Canadian press report in the Ottawa Journal:
(Text):
Mr. Diefenbaker's proposal on parliamentary change contained two points not previously stated in his campaign to date:
First, appointment of a permanent Speaker of the House of Commons in the British tradition, to remove him from "partisan politics".
His proposals on parliamentary changes were made here as he renewed his criticism of government actions during last year's bitter commons pipe line debate.
He said the government had made the Speaker a "party pawn" during the debate.
In the past the speakership had alternated in each parliament between English and French-speaking members.
"I believe that to preserve parliament both races would agree to putting the Speaker above party politics."
I fully agree with this statement, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that during this session, after the legislation is introduced to deal first of all with the unemployment situation, the government will bring in legislation to appoint Your Honour as permanent speaker.
I wish also to extend my congratulations to the Deputy Speaker and the chairman of

the committee of the whole house. In the past they have performed their duties admirably.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to offer my congratulations to the movers of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Jorgenson and Mr. Fortin). They have both performed admirably the task they had been entrusted with. I also wish to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for his wonderful speech.
Mr. Speaker, I said a while ago that, in my opinion, the two most important problems which are confronting the country at present are unemployment and inflation.
I listened very carefully to the speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and I noticed that he had been rather unfair in his remarks.	He charged the
opposition with offering mere criticisms without submitting any constructive suggestion to alleviate this serious problem. I take exception to the words of the minister, and I would like to quote to this house what he said on January 22, 1959, as recorded on page 188 of Hansard. Here is what he said:
If we had from the members of the opposition the same co-operation and constructive and reasonable suggestions as we get from the provinces and the municipalities and organizations and individuals across this country who are endeavouring to co-operate with us to overcome and alleviate the situation, we would put thousands of people to work. But we are not getting that co-operation from the opposition. All we are getting is destructive criticism.
Well, Mr. Speaker, last year I made in this house some constructive and practical suggestions to solve the unemployment problem in my constituency. For the information of the minister and of other members let me read what I said in my speech of May 22, and I quote page 387 of Hansard:
The speech from the throne announces a vast program of public works throughout the country to help the unemployed. In studying it carefully,
I find that few of them will be carried out in my riding. The problem will not be solved until there is an agreement between the federal, provincial and municipal governments for the undertaking of realistic and useful works to create employment.
I would point out to the minister and to this house that I did not mention only winter works. I mentioned works that could be carried out any time in co-operation with the municipal and provincial governments.
I said:
Well, I am going to suggest works of federal responsibility which could be carried out in the riding of Gatineau. Public wharves could be built on some lakes and rivers. In the Gatineau district

the tourist industry ranks second in importance in the constituency. Thousands of tourists come there each year to spend their vacation, either to rest and admire the natural beauty of our lakes, forests and mountains, or for fishing and hunting. Vacationing attracts thousands of tourists, especially American tourists because part of the constituency is located in the area of the national capital, about 60 miles from the border of the most populous state of the United States, the state of New York. Those tourists complain that there are no public wharves on many lakes, which causes considerable difficulties. The government should start the construction of four wharves for which plans and estimates have been prepared by the Department of Public Works, that is: one on lake St. Marie, one at Maniwaki, one at Val des Bois, and one at Notre Dame de la Salette.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that since then I received an answer from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) and that those four wharves have been refused.
The development of Gatineau park, the only national park in the province of Quebec, might be immediately carried out, which would give employment to hundreds of workless people. Incidentally, I would ask my colleagues in this house, and particularly hon. members from the province of Quebec, to visit Gatineau national park which is unique in the province.
As a matter of fact, it is the only national park in the province of Quebec.
The public park and beach which last year were given to the Federal District Commission by the town of Aylmer might also be developed right away and jobs be created for a great number of unemployed.
Mr. Speaker, I was told by the Federal District Commission that they had not enough money to develop that park. I hope that the government will make available to the new National Capital Commission the money required to develop that park in the beautiful city of Aylmer. I also said:
A vast program of public works to be pursued jointly with the provincial and municipal governments might also be launched.
As I said, the winter work program is not enough, and I submit the government does not make a sufficient contribution to the cost of these municipal projects.
There are roads to build and to improve, bridges to span and protecting walls to erect in order to prevent erosion . . . bridges-
Talking about bridges, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the bridge connecting Hull and Ottawa. It is the first time I have dealt with that subject on the floor of the house. It is an interprovincial bridge. The construction of that bridge does not concern only the federal government but also the provinces of Ontario and Quebec as well as the cities of Ottawa and Hull. I have read in the press that the premier of the province of Quebec had stated that if the
The Address-Mr. Leduc federal government wanted a new bridge between Hull and Ottawa it had but to build it at its own expense.
Mr. Speaker, here is my personal view on that matter, and I leave it with the government. In my opinion, the Quebec government is responsible for part of cost of building that bridge and it should pay its share. If it refuses, this government does not have to pay the share of that province, since the bridge connecting Hull and Ottawa serves not only the city of Hull but also the Pontiac, Gatineau and Labelle ridings, as well as the south shore of the Ottawa river, while the people from Abitibi and north-western Quebec have to use it to get to the federal capital.
The province of Quebec has a responsibility and it should pay its own share, the same as it did for the Calumet island bridge. If the federal government backs up on that point, what will happen of the responsibility of the province of Quebec as far as the water pollution of the Ottawa river is concerned? The province of Ontario and the city of Ottawa are ridding the Ottawa river of the sewers discharging into it. On the other hand, on the Quebec side, the sewage of Aylmer, Deschenes, Hull, Gatineau Point and Gatineau Mills flows into the Ottawa river. How is it possible to solve the problem of water pollution in the Ottawa river if the city of Ottawa is the only one to take steps along these lines? The province of Quebec is responsible for the purifying on the Quebec side of the river. There are other bridges to be built. As my hon. friend the member for Carle-ton (Mr. Bell) mentioned, a bridge between Deschenes and Britannia is essential. The province of Quebec must face its responsibilities and the federal government, in my opinion, unless it intends to make a gift to the province of Quebec, should limit itself to paying its own share only.
Mr. Speaker, I read in the papers over the week-end that the members of the new national capital commission had been appointed. Unfortunately, I do not know personally all those who have been appointed on that commission. However, I would like to congratulate the government for having appointed General Kennedy as chairman of that commission. General Kennedy has done a tremendous job with that commission. I have no doubt that the new members of the commission will do a wonderful job of
416	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Leduc giving to the region a development plan worthy of our national capital. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate Mr. Morin, of the city of Aylmer in my constituency, for having been appointed as a representative of all the municipalities of the province of Quebec on the national capital commission.
I have a few suggestions to make, Mr. Speaker, on the development of the Gatineau park, and I would like at the same time to tell you how happy I was last summer to read in the papers that the right hon. Prime Minister had accepted the house made available to him by the federal district commission on lake Harrington. I am sure the right hon. Prime Minister has been able to rest in that lovely site in my constituency. I know also that the constituents of Gatineau have been pleased to learn through the newspapers that Princess Margaret had spent a few days rest there. Incidentally, I am privileged for not only does the right hon. Prime Minister spend his summer vacation in my constituency, but the Leader of the Opposition also has his summer residence a few miles from Chelsea. As for you, Mr. Speaker, I know you have spent happy hours in Mr. Mackenzie King's former residence.
I said that I had a few suggestions to make with regard to the development of Gatineau park. You all know that the federal district commission is now building a driveway and preparing plans for the full development of that park. It seems to me that the commission should undertake at once the biological study of all lakes in the park and destroy any harmful fish. It would be important also to set up in Gatineau park a fish-breeding station and to stock all these lakes with fish, so that the development program should be complete and that the public might enjoy all the benefits it offers.
Mr. Speaker, it is with great interest that I listened to the speeches delivered by my hon. friends opposite, and I have noted that several of them had made a marvellous discovery. In fact, many of them did not know that there existed in Canada a housing act prior to the coming into power of our hon. friends. According to them, the National Housing Act was a revelation, especially as regards my friend from York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee). Last year, more than 135,000 houses were built. I say to my hon. friend and to his colleagues that in 1955 the then Minister of Public Works, the Hon. Mr. 

Winters, gave in Toronto the key to the thousandth house built under this plan. We had already built, in 1955, one million houses beside all those that had been built under the Veterans' Land Act, and beside all the other houses that had been built during the war to lodge the workers around the plants.
I congratulate the government for having made housing more readily available. But I ask the government: what have you done by way of housing for large families? What have you done to help families with five, six, seven, eight, nine, 10, 12 and 15 children?
What have you done? The answer is quite simple: nothing. You have done nothing whatsoever to help large families find suitable homes. And, Mr. Speaker, you are aware of the problem that faces a man who has a large family and is unemployed in this day and age. You are also aware that property owners dislike large families. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the government could easily make it possible for the heads of large families to own their own home. If there is a particular class of citizens that deserves sympathy and attention on the part of the government, surely it is that of the heads of large families. Are there any people who accept greater sacrifices for their country than those who raise a family of eight, nine, ten, twelve and even fifteen children?

If there is a group of citizens that is entitled to some attention from the government, surely it is the group that supplies the country with men and women to replace the dying generation. If the government really wanted to help large families, it could do so through family allowances. In

my opinion, family allowances, a social measure which was adopted by the Liberals and supported by certain Conservatives, are the ideal way to help large families. The hon. members will probably applaud at my statement, and I am proud to make such a statement, to the effect that in my constituency, the unemployment situation is less severe this year than last year. Mr. Speaker,
as the member of parliament for the historic county of Durham in the province of Ontario I rise at this very late hour to take part in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In doing so I wish to express admiration for and extend most hearty congratulations to the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) and the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin), not only for their very able and most inspiring statements but also for their having been granted the signal honour of being the mover and seconder of this address.
Traditionally the gracious throne speech itself sets forth the intent of the government of the day with respect to its actions in the ensuing parliament and describes what it proposes to do for the people of the country. Although that is traditional I believe that on this occasion there is more than tradition involved. I feel that this particular throne speech does much more. The words of the gracious speech are quite clear to all those who wish to understand. These are the positive words of a government that knows the problems of the Canadian people and is taking effective steps to meet those problems. The government is doing for the people of the country the very best that it is possible to do at this time.
There has been criticism of all sorts from the opposition benches and in the particular instance of the criticism launched by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) the critical comment has been lengthy. Such comments, however, have not brought out anything of which the government is not aware, as far as I can determine, nor has it been of a type that could be considered constructive. I might also say it does not give to the Canadian people the impression that the Leader of the Opposition or his party could do anything better than is being done. In fact, in my opinion a great deal of the criticism has been woefully weak and although hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken at great length on a variety of topics some very important matters have been barely mentioned. I refer particularly to the subject of agriculture.
Agriculture is of the greatest importance to Canada as a whole and is of particular importance to large sections of our popula-

The Address-Mr. Vivian tion from coast to coast, not excluding the county of Durham. In contrast to the lack of constructive critical comment from the opposition benches this government has been prepared to state its recognition that while it has done a great deal for agriculture in the last 18 months a great deal more needs to be done to give the agriculturists, our farmers, a fairer share of the national income. In other words, much has been done to improve the lot of the farmer compared with what was done under the former Liberal regime but further steps are needed and some will now be taken.
I should like at this time to quote the intention of the government with respect to agriculture as expressed in the words of the speech from the throne:
Additional legislation in the field of agriculture will be recommended. A measure will be laid before you to institute a system of crop insurance in co-operation with such provinces as so desire. You will also be invited to make a comprehensive review and revision of the legislation concerning farm credit, in order that credit may be more effective in assisting in the development and maintenance of an efficient and prosperous agriculture.
Surely this is a real advance in what I consider to be the very long road that must be travelled before our farmers are really in receipt of their fair share of the national income, a goal which at least we on this side of the house hope will be attained.
While hon. gentlemen opposite did not refer to agriculture with any great frequency there were closely related matters which were touched upon superficially-and I gathered the impression in some instances, rather insincerely-and on the odd occasion in contradiction to the words of hon. gentlemen spoken other than in this house. However, much of the comment made by the Leader of Opposition has been and will be refuted by ministers of the crown when dealing with their own departments and by other hon. members in relation to their own constituencies. I shall, therefore, limit my observations on these criticisms to the comments I have made and comment favourably on certain intentions of the government as contained in the gracious speech.
One important reference in the throne speech was that to the commonwealth trade and economic conference held in Montreal last September. I noted with interest the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition on this subject and also what he said about a not altogether unrelated matter, that of

Canadian-United States relations. The speech from the throne contains the following words:
In response to suggestions put forward by my government, a commonwealth trade and economic conference was held in Montreal last September. This meeting, one of the most important in the history of the commonwealth, was attended by ministers representing the self-governing nations of the commonwealth and the countries now looking forward to obtaining full sovereignty. A large measure of agreement was reached on trade and economic matters. This has led to far-reaching decisions on the part of the United Kingdom and other countries to restore convertibility of their currencies and to remove restrictions on imports.
Mr. Speaker, this was not just another conference of the kind held frequently since the last war under the Liberal regime. This conference was probably the most carefully prepared one of its kind ever held, in the opinion of experts who have attended many of them. In the scope of its representation alone there was a breadth which had not been equalled, because there were delegates not only from the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa but also from India, Pakistan, Ceylon, Ghana, the federation of Malaya and Nyasaland. In addition, a number of colonial territories were represented to the United Kingdom in an advisory capacity; Nigeria, the West Indies, Kenya, Tanganyika, Uganda, Sierra Leone and Hong Kong. Incidentally, this was the first conference at which new members of the commonwealth in Asia and Africa outnumbered the older members. The conference dealt with an unusually wide range of topics as it concerned itself with more than commonwealth inter-relations. Its themes included the role of an expanding commonwealth in an expanding world and, with this, there was a realization of the crucial role which the commonwealth is playing in fostering world economic prosperity and in promoting the progress of its less developed member countries.
In spite of the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), I submit that this was a conference unique in its assembly. There were other words used in the course of critical comment which I think have been overdone, and I refer to the somewhat quibbling attitude toward the words "led" and "foreshadowed". The fact remains that after long periods of discussion and consideration prior to this conference, currencies have been made convertible, and I suggest that a major contributing factor to this event and to other matters of great importance was the large measure of agreement which was reached at Montreal on the widest possible range of topics.

This conference, however, did not limit its interest to commonwealth co-operation but sought the participation of other countries. In section II of the report of the Montreal conference dealing with commodity problems and agriculture, paragraph 45 of the whole, it is stated, and I quote:
We recognize that, for the most part, effective action will require the participation of the important producing and consuming countries throughout the world.
Then I wish to underline the following, which is still part of the quotation:
It is our hope that countries outside the commonwealth will accept our objectives and be prepared to join with us in our work.
We know that two of the great powers outside the commonwealth are the Soviet union and the United States. What can be done with respect to trade relations with the Soviet union is a mystery, but it is certainly no secret that the co-operation of the United States is essential to the success of many of the commonwealth endeavours. I would point out that after the commonwealth conference an event happened in the second
The Address-Mr. Vivian committee of the United Nations during the thirteenth general assembly which is an example of improved relations not only with the commonwealth but with the United States, because at this point the Canadian delegation was able to obtain the full support of the delegation of the United States for the acceptance of language in a resolution on international commodity trade which went farther than the United States has ever been prepared to go before. This, I submit, is a real result, and it is only one example of the benefits which have flowed from the Montreal conference.
I do not understand, in the light of this and other examples, how the Leader of the Opposition can justify the position he took in minimizing the value of this last conference on trade and economic matters in Montreal.
On motion of Mr. Vivian the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: FREIGHT RATE STRUCTURE INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
1.	Did the government instruct the board of transport commissioners to make a thorough investigation into the freight rate structure in April, 1948?
2.	If so, what were the terms of reference?
3.	Has the investigation taken place and have interim reports been made from time to time?
4.	If so, on what date and with reference to what category or classification of rates?
5.	When will the investigation be terminated?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
1.	Yes.
2.	The board was directed to undertake a general freight rates investigation along the lines indicated in order in council P.C. 1487 dated April 7, 1948, subject to such special statutory provisions as affect freight rates. The order in council is reproduced in the interim report of the board to the governor in council dated March 25, 1955, tabled on May 3, 1955.
3.	Yes.
4.	Public hearings commenced in 1951 and have been held on numerous subsequent dates and are continuing. Interim reports to the governor in council were made by the board, dated respectively March 25, 1955, September 23, 1957 and December 22, 1958. The first report had reference to class rates and the freight classification in connection therewith, mileage commodity rates and specific commodity rates; the second report had reference to additional mileage commodity rates and the third report had reference to other mileage commodity rates and specific commodity rates.
5.	The investigation is being made jointly with the board's equalization of freight rates required by section 336 of the Railway Act. The board estimates that it will require two to three years to complete it.

subsubtopic: COLD STORAGE WAREHOUSE STATISTICS
speechtext:
1.	What is the total number of cold storage warehouses in Canada, and what cubic space is available?
2.	How many are used exclusively or in the main for (a) fish and fish products; (b) agricultural products; (c) general or variety of products?
3.	What cubic space is available for (a) freezing; (b) cooling?
4.	What was the percentage of occupancy of the space available for (a) fish and fish products; (b) agricultural products; (c) general or variety of products, for each of the months of 1958?

Questions
Answer by: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister
of Agriculture):
1.	3,068 cold storage warehouses in Canada containing 142,696,294 cubic feet of refrigerated space.
2.	(a) 249 warehouses storing in the main, fish and fish products, (b) 1,969 warehouses storing in the main, agricultural products, (c) 850 warehouses are classed as general, that is, storing all products.
3.	(a) 61,292,705 cubic feet of space for storage of frozen commodities in bulk, (b) 85,705,302 cubic feet of space for storage of fresh produce in bulk at temperatures above freezing.
4.	The dominion bureau of statistics do not require cold storage warehouses to report what percentage of the space is occupied. They do require, however, a statement of the quantities of certain goods in storage and this information is published in various forms, many of which are on a monthly basis. The Department of Agriculture receives voluntary confidential reports showing the percentage occupancy of warehouses which represent about one-third of the total available refrigerated space in Canada. These cold storages are located at various points throughout Canada and the information received indicates that cold storage occupancy on a national basis during 1958 ranged from 55 per cent to 88 per cent for "freezer" space and 48 per cent to 77 per cent for "cooler" space.
Note: Answers to 1, 2 and 3 are taken from "Directory of Cold Storage Warehouses in Canada", prepared by the Department of Agriculture and published in March 1958.
